Following Donald Trump’s election as US President, the global economy faces heightened uncertainty. Under the new US administration, there could be two fundamental shifts in the direction of US policy — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to deglobalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, emerging market economies face heightened risks amid a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar and the possible adoption of trade protectionist measures by the US. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose alongside their US dollar counterparts. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained favourable, and overall loan growth accelerated further in the second half of 2016. The residential property market showed signs of correction immediately after the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, but has picked up recently. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes and, more broadly, US policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and their potential impact on local interest rates. Following Donald Trump’s election as US President, the global economy faces heightened uncertainty. Not only did the election outcome surprise the market, but the related market reactions were also unexpected. In particular, expectations that measures introduced by Trump, such as tax reform, increased infrastructure spending and deregulation, would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. Under the new US administration, there could be two fundamental shifts in the direction of US policy — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to deglobalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. However, the Trump tax cuts anticipated by the market may not provide the expected boost to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity already close to its potential, fiscal stimulus may provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth while exacerbating upside risks to US inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (Fed) would therefore significantly accelerate the pace of monetary tightening, long-term bond yields have already risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, rising trade protectionism would create a “lose-lose” outcome for both the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would result in market distortions that undermine overall welfare, hamper global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the still-fragile economic recovery in Europe. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows arising from faster US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation has increased. This could weigh on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of abrupt capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration and concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, leading to broad-based and significant increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings suggest that the influence of the US Treasury market on sovereign bond markets has deepened since the 2013 “taper tantrum”, and that US interest rate hikes and tighter financial conditions would have significant impacts on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 alongside a recovery in exports, while market volatility arising from concerns about potential policy changes under the new US administration, including currency depreciation and higher sovereign bond yields in the region, only began to stabilise gradually in early 2017. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but faces increased risks and uncertainties. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation and heightened financial market volatility could lead to tighter financial conditions. Meanwhile, the US may introduce protectionist policies that could affect regional economies, although the actual impact remains uncertain. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private-sector business spending. Although the economy continued to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainty remains over the Mainland’s growth outlook. In particular, given the Government’s determination to curb housing price increases, the real estate sector’s contribution to growth may decline this year if the property market continues to cool. Meanwhile, the continued advancement of economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty over the near-term economic outlook. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private-sector economic activity, some concerns remain in the market about the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given that M1 growth accelerated while M2 growth slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) explores the factors that may have led to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the markedly faster growth of M1 relative to M2 was mainly attributable to monetary easing in recent years, which reduced the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, as well as increased economic uncertainty, which may have raised precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth increased from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity boosted investment growth in the fourth quarter. Externally, merchandise export growth increased alongside improved regional trade flows, while exports of services grew steadily amid a recovery in trade-related and transportation services. As imports of goods and services grew faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half. Alongside the pickup in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. The Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2–3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook continues to face significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong’s external demand. Amid appreciation pressures on the US dollar and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, global financial conditions are expected to become less supportive of the real economy and could result in tighter domestic financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of a financial conditions index for Hong Kong to facilitate the monitoring of domestic financial conditions. Local inflationary pressures have remained moderate since the second half of 2016, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly reflecting fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, although it weakened occasionally following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered. Alongside US dollar appreciation, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Given the sizeable Monetary Base, Hong Kong interbank rates remained low, but rose from October onwards owing to year-end funding demand and the need to catch up with the US dollar interest rate hike. Accordingly, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage rate edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. The growth was supported by stronger domestic economic activity and increased year-end funding demand from multinational corporations. Domestic loan growth picked up slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a modest decline in the first half. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans increased by 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayments of foreign currency loans. Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting faster deposit growth than loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio fell markedly to 63.8% amid strong growth in US dollar deposits. Amid a strong US dollar, both the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool, comprising outstanding customer deposits and certificates of deposit, consolidated further alongside other offshore renminbi markets, while volatility in offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates increased markedly. Nevertheless, banks’ renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds from uncertainty over renminbi exchange rate movements. Alongside improving global market conditions, the Hong Kong equity market closed sharply higher during the review period. Although the outcome of the US presidential election was unexpected, the market impact was short-lived. This was mainly because investor optimism over fiscal stimulus measures under the Trump administration drove global equity markets higher. While benefiting from this, the local market displayed cautious optimism, possibly reflecting concerns about a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland economic outlook, uncertainty over renminbi policy and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply towards the end of last year and their spreads over US Treasuries widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar debt market continued to expand steadily during the review period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi debt market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, although new bond issuance for the year as a whole was still lower than in the preceding year. Looking ahead, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi debt markets would come under pressure if global investors reversed their earlier search-for-yield strategies. With US trade policy remaining uncertain and the renminbi exchange rate likely to remain volatile, the outlook for both debt markets over the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties. The residential property market showed signs of correction immediately after the Government introduced the new stamp duty measure, but has picked up recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the Government raised the stamp duty rate uniformly to 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets declined in the following two months. However, transaction volumes have increased recently, partly reflecting increased launches of primary-market developments by property developers. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, albeit at a slower pace.

Following Donald Trump’s unexpected election as US President, uncertainty surrounding US policies increased. Although market attention focused on the short-term benefits from potentially large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is already close to its potential. Fiscal stimulus may therefore provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth, while further intensifying upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks facing emerging market economies are increasing amid capital outflow pressures arising from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures would also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, with export volumes also increasing recently. Nevertheless, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, while downside risks to economic growth have increased. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improving private-sector business spending. Economic rebalancing continued, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, although the continued economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty surrounding the near-term economic outlook. Given the Government’s determination to curb housing price increases, the property sector’s contribution to economic growth may also decline this year if the property market continues to cool. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Global financial markets reacted strongly to Donald Trump’s unexpected election as US President. In particular, market expectations that the Trump administration’s policies, including tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending and deregulation, would boost US economic growth and inflation drove up major equity markets (Chart 2.1). Consequently, rising market expectations of US inflation and interest rate hikes led to a sharp increase in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Chart 2.1 Equity market indices in selected advanced economies Nevertheless, the anticipated Trump tax cuts may not have as positive an impact on US economic growth as the market expects. While shifting the policy mix towards fiscal easing would help alleviate the heavy burden on monetary easing, whether this is an appropriate time to implement fiscal easing is debatable, given the current stage of the US economic cycle. Although US economic growth has moderated in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, while the unemployment rate in February was in line with the US Fed’s estimated natural rate of unemployment of 4.7%, indicating that US economic activity is close to its potential. As the US economy is currently in an expansionary phase, the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. Indeed, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital could result in lower tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with diminishing spare capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth could push up inflation, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited. Meanwhile, other factors, including rising oil and commodity prices and potential trade protectionist measures such as the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could also intensify upside risks to US inflation. Despite the increased risk of higher US inflation, the US Fed has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and inclined to maintain its ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have already risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market projections of the future Federal Funds rate have been revised upwards to levels close to the median US Fed projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the US Fed’s longer-run projection (Chart 2.2). Therefore, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger significant market volatility. While financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of stronger US economic growth driven by potentially expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, longer-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further increase in US Government debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfil its campaign promises by adopting trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would create market distortions that undermine overall welfare, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future Federal Funds rate projections: US Fed versus market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and impediment to the European economic recovery. Although economic conditions in the Euro area gradually improved, with real GDP growing moderately by 1.7% year on year in the fourth quarter, only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, economic activity in the Euro area remained only slightly above its pre-global financial crisis level, in contrast to the stronger US economic recovery (Chart 2.3). Since the United Kingdom’s decision to leave the European Union last summer, markets have been concerned about the eventual disintegration of the Euro area. Although Italy’s economic and political situation appeared to stabilise after the formation of a new government and the implementation of measures to rescue the banking sector, the upcoming elections in Germany and France, and possibly Italy, could become political flashpoints against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly because of increased political uncertainty, European sovereign bond yields continued to rise and corporate bond spreads widened, particularly in peripheral countries. This could create an adverse feedback loop with the real economy and weigh on real business investment in the Euro area. Chart 2.3 Real GDP in major advanced economies In Japan, upward revisions to real GDP in recent quarters and a rise in year-on-year growth to 1.6% in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicate that the economic recovery was stronger than previously expected. However, partly because of structural problems in the labour market, wage growth remained slow, resulting in weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent sharp depreciation of the Japanese yen implies that the downward pressure on “new core” goods inflation from the earlier appreciation of the yen should begin to subside. Coupled with the stronger-than-expected recovery, this suggests an improving near-term inflation outlook, with “new core” inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, likely to have bottomed out after declining to 0.1% in December. Nevertheless, amid long-term and structural headwinds, growth is likely to remain slow, while inflation expectations remain at around 0.5%–0.6%, below their level when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014. The risk that inflation will fail to reach the Bank of Japan’s medium-term target of 2% therefore remains. For other countries, particularly emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth through the trade channel may be smaller because of reduced US imports since the global financial crisis and the possibility of US protectionist policies. Meanwhile, faster US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation would tighten financial conditions and exacerbate downside risks to the economy. This could weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration, coupled with concerns over a sharp rise in energy prices, led to a repricing of inflation risks and a broad-based, significant increase in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with GDP growing modestly and inflation rising across the region. Real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable, supported by steady private consumption in many regional economies. Meanwhile, exports generally increased modestly from their lows in 2015, benefiting not only from stabilising growth in China but also from improving conditions in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters such as Malaysia and Indonesia, the recovery in commodity prices provided an additional boost. Other major exporters, such as South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, also regained momentum on the back of growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — Producer price inflation generally trended upwards as commodity prices, particularly oil prices, recovered. While this would increase industrial costs and possibly consumer spending, consumption and investment growth could benefit from a reduced risk of prolonged deflation. Faster producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, although the actual impact will depend on the extent to which increases in producer prices are passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for CPI inflation suggest that inflation in many regional economies, while still slightly below their respective central banks’ 2017 inflation targets, will rise closer to the target levels (Chart 2.4). Central banks in East Asia generally maintained their accommodative monetary policy stances and kept interest rates unchanged, except for Indonesia, which cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to support growth. Chart 2.4 Headline CPI inflation, forecasts and central bank targets in East Asia Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign exchange market — Following the US presidential election, most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar as investors expected higher US inflation. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies depreciated by less or even appreciated slightly following the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Spot foreign exchange depreciation against the US dollar versus changes in nominal effective exchange rates following the US election Bond and equity markets — Asset prices briefly declined after the US presidential election but soon stabilised. The spreads between East Asian sovereign bond yields and US Treasury yields increased. However, as markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined, although they remained above their pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, the spreads narrowed from their post-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign bond yields and US Treasury yields Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the “taper tantrum” in mid-2013. Inflows resumed in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain steady, although still below its historical average. Given the increased uncertainty surrounding US Government policies and the US Fed’s possible policy responses, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. Sharp increases in the US dollar and yields could attract funds from the region to the US, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, especially those already at elevated valuations. The resulting tightening of financial conditions would also place repayment pressure on corporates with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. From a macroeconomic perspective, broad-based global interest rate hikes would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, weighing not only on aggregate demand in the short term but also potentially affecting long-term potential growth. Finally, regional exporters face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies under the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in the region’s major export sectors, including electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, clothing and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these sectors have been accompanied by substantial job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalising US manufacturing could pose significant risks to regional exporters.

Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, driven by faster growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activities. In view of the increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. Inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained, supported by stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP grew by 1.2% in the fourth quarter, slightly faster than the 0.8% growth in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly reflecting improved consumer confidence and resilient labour market conditions, private consumption growth accelerated and became the main driver of GDP growth. Building and construction activities also turned buoyant, supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport. However, weak corporate capital expenditure reduced the contribution of aggregate investment spending to GDP growth. Externally, both exports and imports of goods grew faster alongside increased regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).22 Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly because of strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions by major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). Indeed, unemployment rates in several major sectors declined during the second half, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector showed signs of stabilisation. Total employment reached a record high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment. Coupled with the rise in the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate resulting from the strong US dollar, this will restrain Hong Kong’s export performance. On the domestic front, while stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately amid the drag from rising interest rates. Building and construction activities should grow steadily as housing supply increases and several planned infrastructure projects commence, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will weigh on corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth in the range of 2% to 3% in 2017, while private-sector analysts’ forecasts average 2.0%. The growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those arising from the external environment. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, while potential trade protectionist policies may pose headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar fund flows. In addition, US interest rate normalisation will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation has remained moderate overall, despite an increase in its quarter-on-quarter momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before edging down to 2.4% in January. The pickup in inflation momentum mainly reflected increases in tradable goods prices and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods price inflation rose from negative territory in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by prices of basic food and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index increased from the third quarter onwards as the decline in private residential rentals narrowed and public housing rentals were raised in September 2016, before moderating slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major component Chart 3.6 Composite Consumer Price Index rental component and market rentals In the near term, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained amid weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures. Imported inflation should remain low, as the strong Hong Kong dollar partly offsets the impact of recovering global commodity prices (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby contain inflation in services components. Despite the tight labour market, wage growth was modest in recent quarters, with real wages per capita rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before declining by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against the backdrop of cautious business sentiment amid persistent uncertainty in the external environment, increases in labour costs should be restrained. In addition, given the weak retail sales performance in recent months, growth in retail property rentals is expected to remain moderate. Moreover, the impact of the earlier easing in private residential rentals will gradually feed through, also helping to alleviate inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline in 2017. The Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate for the year at 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% recorded in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour costs and real wages per capita The inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if US inflation accelerates under the Trump administration, US interest rates may rise faster than expected, potentially pushing up local mortgage rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. Meanwhile, appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak and reduce Hong Kong’s attractiveness to inbound visitors. On the upside, faster-than-expected global economic expansion may accelerate Hong Kong’s economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the revised Statutory Minimum Wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which may further increase inflation, although the actual impact of such cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose alongside their US dollar counterparts. Partly reflecting the improved domestic economic environment, overall lending continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalisation, uncertainty over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to broad-based declines in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13–14 December 2016 heightened market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly afterwards. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened alongside other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening from mid-February as market expectations of a US rate hike in March increased. During the review period, the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund-flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators Alongside the strong US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilising more recently (Chart 4.3). With only a mild impact from the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) closely tracked the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-residents’ investments in equity and debt securities registered net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by Hong Kong banks’ increased holdings of US debt securities, residents’ debt investments recorded sizeable outflows that more than offset the investment inflows from non-residents. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated portfolio investment outflows in the final quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election and expectations of faster US interest rate hikes put pressure on local financial markets and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data indicated inflow pressures on portfolio investment in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2017, partly reflecting improved global financial market performance amid investor optimism about expansionary fiscal policies in the US. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process and elections in EU member states may lead to greater fund-flow volatility. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading initially exceeded southbound trading following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite higher US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable and increased further by 1.7% in the second half, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and Government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained broadly stable at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within the total, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding EFBNs increased correspondingly, owing to the additional issuance of HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base As the domestic economy became more firmly established, growth in the Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HK$M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of HK$M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand amid stronger domestic economic activities and a rebound in IPO activities. Analysed by its counterparts, the growth in HK$M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively represented money creation arising from credit expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in HK$M3 and its counterparts On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits registered a stronger increase of 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). By contrast, deposits in other foreign currencies contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, growth in total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) accelerated to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, bringing full-year growth to 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Banks’ wholesale funding costs increased in the fourth quarter of 2016 amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, they rose partly because of year-end funding demand and a catch-up with increases in US dollar interbank interest rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) increased by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards alongside the US dollar yield curve, with the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rising by around 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at the end of December. Moving into early 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined as funding demand eased, while longer-term Hong Kong Government Bond yields also edged down alongside US Treasury yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates and 10-year Government Bond yield Owing to the banking system’s sizeable deposit base, increases in retail interest rates were relatively small. Banks’ average funding cost, as measured by the composite interest rate, remained low, rising by only 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). Amid relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage business, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 alongside HIBORs. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Looking ahead, the pace of increases in local interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalisation, the scale of fund outflows and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on local interest rates, together with an increase in the Hong Kong dollar REER alongside the US dollar exchange rate, may reduce the support provided by domestic financial conditions to the real economy. Box 4 discusses the construction of a financial conditions index for Hong Kong to monitor domestic financial conditions. Driven by stronger domestic economic activities and increased cross-border financing demand, total lending rose further by 4.2% in the second half, following growth of 2.2% in the first half (Chart 4.10). As economic growth momentum strengthened, growth in domestic loans edged up from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after declining slightly in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end funding demand from multinational corporations. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also recorded moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayments of foreign currency loans. For 2016 as a whole, total lending grew moderately by 6.5%, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analysed by economic sector, domestic loans showed mixed performance in the second half (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial concerns and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, reflecting to some extent strong financing demand driven by better growth prospects in these sectors. Loans for building, construction and property development also grew at a faster pace alongside increased private-sector construction activities. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade financing and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans by selected sector Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half, from 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, increased by 7.2%, partly reflecting the improved economic environment (Chart 4.11), while growth in residential mortgage loans accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting buoyant residential property transactions between July and October. Consequently, the household debt-to-GDP ratio also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt-to-GDP ratio and its components Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly stable. Reflecting faster deposit growth than loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at the end of June 2016 to 77.1% at the end of the year (Chart 4.13). Meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 61.4% to 59.9% at the end of the year, with the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio falling sharply to 63.8% amid strong growth in US dollar deposits. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit ratios Credit growth will be subject to uncertainties in the period ahead amid expectations of higher interest rates and a rapidly changing macro-financial environment. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook indicated that loan demand would remain soft in the near term. Both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened amid US dollar appreciation (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of late 2016, closing at a yearly low of 6.98 against the US dollar at the end of 2016. The CNH interbank market again experienced liquidity-tightening pressure in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary funding demand ahead of the year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight CNH HIBOR surged to 61.3% on 6 January 2017. Higher CNH funding costs subsequently led to the unwinding of short CNH positions, driving a rebound in the CNH exchange rate in early January 2017 and turning the CNH-CNY discount into a premium. Since mid-January, the CNH and CNY exchange rates have stabilised somewhat and liquidity conditions have gradually improved, with the overnight and three-month CNH HIBORs declining to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, retail banks’ profitability improved compared with the same period in 2015, due to increases in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decrease in loan impairment charges. Banks’ capital positions and asset quality also remained sound. Although HIBORs rose notably following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity conditions of the banking sector remained sound. Retail banks’ funding costs stayed stable and low, supported by a large retail deposit base. Nevertheless, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, particularly the risk of significant fund outflows and their subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. Moreover, given the continued rise in the leverage of non-local corporates, a sharp increase in interest rates may lead to a deterioration in banks’ asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against system-wide risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be raised to 1.875% from 1 January 2018. Retail banks’ profitability improved, with the return on assets rising to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 (the red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was attributable to increases in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decrease in loan impairment charges. For 2016 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose to 1.10% from 1.05% in 2015. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Hong Kong’s wholesale funding costs rose notably following the resumption of US interest rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose markedly by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained low by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates Nevertheless, the overall impact of the US interest rate hike on retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained modest. This was because retail deposits were the main source of funding for retail banks, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low despite the interest rate hike. Against this backdrop, after staying at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year, the composite interest rate, which measures the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar pattern. Although banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, their average deposit funding costs in the retail market increased by a smaller 11 basis points. Overall, licensed banks’ average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 17 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The greater and faster rise in HIBORs than in Hong Kong banks’ funding costs may benefit some retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted HIBOR-based mortgage loans in recent years, and higher interest rates on such loans may help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there were signs that some banks had narrowed their mortgage spreads over the benchmark rate and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. Over the longer term, as the US raises interest rates further, banks may soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, which would affect their funding costs and have a more significant impact on their net interest margins. Banks’ capitalisation remained strong and well above international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained high at 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Therefore, capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with the data up to December 2012. The liquidity conditions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, remained sound during the reporting period. Although the average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions edged down from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016 to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016, it remained high (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained well above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector was able to withstand liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for retail banks. The share of customer deposits in banks’ total liabilities increased from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks As retail banks’ total loans and advances and total deposits grew at similar rates during the reporting period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). During the same period, the Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratios also remained broadly unchanged. Chart 5.8 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of retail banks Although the interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks increased slightly, it remained at a low level. Estimates suggest that, under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions could decline by an amount equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base in December 2016 (Chart 5.9). Nevertheless, given that the pace of US interest rate normalisation may be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. The asset quality of retail banks’ loan portfolios remained sound during the reporting period, with the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans staying low at 0.72% and 0.53% respectively at the end of December 2016. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks Although asset quality remained sound by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to monitor the external environment; as the assessment in Box 5 shows, the rapid growth in the banking sector’s loans for use outside Hong Kong since the global financial crisis indicates that banks’ asset quality has become more susceptible to the external environment. Banks had mixed expectations regarding near-term credit growth. According to the HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2016, although most surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the share of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). The credit risk associated with unsecured personal loans remained contained in the second half of 2016, with the annualised credit card charge-off ratio and the delinquency ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio for credit card lending and bankruptcy petitions Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at the end of December. The average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This ratio was well below the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt-servicing index for new mortgages47 rose from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (the red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average size of new mortgage loans (Chart 5.13). Continued interest rate normalisation in the US may further increase household debt-servicing burdens. A sensitivity test shows that, if interest rates were to rise by 300 basis points with other factors remaining unchanged, the index could rise markedly to 67.3 within four quarters.48 Banks should remain vigilant against the risk of a continued increase in household debt-servicing burdens. Chart 5.12 Average loan-to-value ratio of new mortgage loans and household debt-servicing burden Chart 5.13 New mortgage loans of surveyed authorized institutions The pace of US interest rate hikes remained a key factor affecting the credit risk of corporate loans. However, the actual impact on the asset quality of individual banks depends on the characteristics of their corporate loan portfolios. In particular, our assessment based on the accounting data of Hong Kong-listed non-financial corporates found that the leverage trends of local and non-local corporates diverged markedly after the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates being more susceptible to debt-servicing problems.50 Banks should assess the impact of interest rate hikes on the credit risk of their exposures to non-local corporates. As markets reassessed US inflation risks, global financial markets saw renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January peaks, completely erasing the notable gains recorded at the beginning of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global equity markets amid low volatility over the past two years was underpinned by market expectations of a Goldilocks scenario featuring continued steady economic growth and low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations are being challenged by the risks of tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar weakened, while markets continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. Following a modest slowdown in the middle of last year, both housing price growth and transaction volumes picked up in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may increase volatility in Hong Kong’s fund flows. Given uncertainties in financial markets, the normalisation of US monetary policy and lingering geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant to the risks of greater interest rate volatility and potential fund outflows. In particular, given the continued increase in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact of larger-than-expected interest rate increases on asset quality. Following more than two years during which the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) hovered at low levels, global financial markets saw renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January peaks, with the S&P 500 Index at one point dropping by more than 10%, completely erasing the notable gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was prompted by signs that the global economic recovery could exert pressure on persistently low US wages and prices, potentially leading the US Federal Reserve (Fed) to accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rally in global equity markets over the past two years was built on market expectations that favourable economic conditions would persist. Global growth momentum continued to strengthen in the second half of 2017, with a synchronised pickup in economic activity across advanced and emerging market economies. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package comprising tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and individual tax rules, raising market expectations that the robust US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite stronger activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further entrenching market expectations that global interest rates would stay low for an extended period. Against this background, global asset markets rallied notably in 2017, with US equity markets in particular repeatedly reaching record highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. Beyond the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its potential output, and the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy more rapidly. Meanwhile, as the tax cuts will result in a larger fiscal deficit, the US may issue more Treasury securities in the future, which is expected to add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Fed continues to advance its balance-sheet normalisation. Outside the US, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect their central banks to scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If realised, this would result in synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also cloud the outlook for global economic growth. The US Government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given the aforementioned uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, the sustainability of the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets is in question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether cyclical growth in global demand and the expected increase in the US fiscal deficit resulting from tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); coupled with an expected increase in the term premium arising from the Fed’s balance-sheet normalisation, this could raise long-term interest rates and weigh on asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies also enjoyed a favourable environment of robust growth and moderate inflation. Alongside the favourable economic performance and optimistic outlook, capital inflows accelerated and financial markets rallied. However, this favourable outlook is subject to downside risks arising from tightening global liquidity as major central banks proceed with monetary policy normalisation in tandem; the US Government’s inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and potentially tighter offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporations repatriate substantial profits in response to the one-off “deemed repatriation” provision under the country’s tax reform. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of fund flows, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being most vulnerable to tightening financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure investment and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. Meanwhile, signs of the rise of the “new economy” became increasingly evident, with sectors such as high-value-added manufacturing and services displaying strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the “new economy” can help offset the near-term pressure on growth arising from further advances in structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, banks’ exposures to corporates in industries with excess capacity remained contained as banks tightened their lending standards, while shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment ability appear to have tightened, possibly because of reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017 amid stabilising economic conditions and receding risks. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for 2017 as a whole, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Private consumption continued to grow robustly in the second half of 2017, supported by favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices. Aggregate investment spending also rebounded on increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, supported by stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods remained a drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018, supported by private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth of 3%–4% and 3.0% respectively for 2018. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, Mainland China’s economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and developments in local asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a nearly 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained contained. However, quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum showed signs of edging up in recent months, with prices of both tradable goods and services increasing. Looking ahead, underlying inflation may edge up to a still-moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through of increases in fresh-letting private residential rentals. Funding demand arising from initial public offering activities and seasonal funding needs tightened liquidity conditions, while increased unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions caused the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017. In early 2018, the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable despite turbulence in global financial markets, particularly equity markets. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. HIBORs faced upward pressure between September and December 2017, mainly due to funding demand arising from initial public offering activities and banks’ prudent liquidity management towards the year-end. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points from six months earlier to 0.25% and 1.26% respectively. After edging down in early January 2018, HIBORs remained broadly stable and were unaffected by the recent correction in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average lending rate for new mortgages followed the upward trend in short-term HIBORs and rose to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks’ funding costs remained generally low after a temporary increase in October due to initial public offering activities, with the composite interest rate ending December at 0.38%. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy normalisation continues, while fund flow volatility may increase if global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly. Total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1% in 2017. Following strong growth of 10.2% in the first half of the year, loan growth moderated to 5.3% in the second half. In particular, growth in domestic loans to most sectors and loans for use outside Hong Kong both slowed. The moderation in foreign currency loan growth partly reflected higher US dollar funding costs. Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly, supported by the favourable domestic economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio increased in the second half of 2017 to 82.7% at the year-end, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, owing to the relatively slow growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at the year-end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened notably against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Following a modest decline in the first half of the year, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool, comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit, edged up in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations of the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the value of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong picked up in the second half. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from advances in the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The momentum of synchronised strengthening in the global economy since late 2016 showed no signs of abating. The improved growth outlook drove global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking the end of the calm conditions in financial markets over the preceding two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tighter global financial conditions and a range of policy and event risks will continue to cloud the global outlook. Amid a tight labour market, US tax cuts may accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the US Federal Reserve (Fed) to quicken the pace of monetary tightening. As the US Fed continues to advance its balance sheet normalisation, increased US Treasury issuance to finance the tax cuts may add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The spectre of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, supported by strong export performance and stable domestic demand. However, despite the optimistic economic outlook, there were also various downside risks, such as potentially greater-than-expected tightening in global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies and geopolitical tensions. The materialisation of these downside risks would also increase the risk of a reversal in fund flows. Policymakers are facing multiple challenges, as they need to guard against risks to economic growth while limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remained positive but was subject to uncertainties, partly depending on the extent to which the rapid growth of the “new economy” could offset the near-term pressure on growth arising from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks receded, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the cyclical economic upswing became increasingly entrenched from late 2016, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the US recorded solid growth in investment and exports, supported by improving private-sector sentiment and a sharp depreciation of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also experienced broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilisation of global commodity prices and stronger import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from corporate and personal income tax relief. In view of the ongoing cyclical upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts As growth momentum strengthened in the Euro area and Japan, market expectations that global monetary policy divergence would narrow, together with a more optimistic global growth outlook, boosted risk appetite and fund inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite three interest rate hikes by the US Fed during the year and the commencement of balance sheet normalisation, the US Dollar Index still declined by nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, notwithstanding the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in the major advanced economies remained subdued and below their central banks’ targets, leading markets until recently to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise throughout 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly reaching record highs and pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the “dot-com bubble” in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher fiscal deficits and inflation had driven US long-term Treasury yields steadily higher, calling into question the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. Following the release of stronger-than-expected growth in US average hourly earnings for January 2018, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index at one point fell by more than 10% from its 26 January peak, completely erasing its notable gains since the beginning of the year, and remained under pressure after the US Government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index at one point jumping to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the low-volatility environment that had persisted over the preceding two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the short-term equity market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to US long-term bond yields and possible monetary tightening by other major central banks could all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, thereby clouding the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform includes certain provisions expected to provide a short-term cyclical boost to private consumption and investment. The major measures under the tax reform include: (1) reductions in corporate and personal income tax rates, (2) temporary full expensing of capital investment, and (3) a one-off “deemed repatriation” provision that helps reduce the incentive for US corporates to retain their overseas profits offshore. While it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its potential, the tax cuts could push US output further above potential, thereby leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise by more than expected, the US Fed may be prompted to quicken the pace of monetary tightening. At present, the path of the Fed funds rate expected by financial markets is shallower than the US Fed’s published projections. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of an abrupt repricing of interest rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Fed funds rate projections Second, given that the tax reform may widen the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase in the future. As the US Fed continues to implement its balance sheet normalisation plan, the term premium is expected to rise; against this backdrop, increased US Treasury issuance may intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Moreover, as market expectations of the passage of the US tax-cut package increased, US inflation expectations had risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). As a result, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield had risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns about increasing Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 Five-year, five-year forward inflation expectations In addition, whether the natural rate of interest (R\*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for an extended period as widely expected is a key consideration. Although estimates of R\* vary, it is generally believed to have declined substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, US R\* may face upside risks in the future because (1) an expected increase in the fiscal deficit could lower the national saving rate, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure could raise the investment rate. An increase in R\*, together with the expected rise in the term premium resulting from the US Fed’s balance sheet normalisation, may presage higher long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R\* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, stronger growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan has led markets to expect their central banks to scale back monetary accommodation. Should this occur, it could signal synchronised tightening in global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies recorded broad-based cyclical expansions (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real GDP recording an eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continued to signal the maintenance of accommodative monetary policies amid subdued inflation, the brighter growth outlooks in the Euro area and Japan (and the continued tightening of Japan’s labour market) had led some market participants to predict a further scaling back of their quantitative easing programmes in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP in selected Euro area member economies Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent recovery in global economic growth and trade.
