The US Government appeared more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, with recent examples including the import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines announced in January 2018 and those on steel and aluminium announced in early March, raising concerns about retaliatory measures by its trading partners. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom and other European Union countries were negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process subject to numerous uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade frictions, they may impede global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions, such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East and latent risks of terrorist attacks, may increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a strong note. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main growth driver, while domestic demand also provided steady support (Chart 2.8). Accelerating recoveries in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted the region’s exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressures remained subdued. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated amid lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained low due to slow wage growth in many economies. Chart 2.9 East Asia: Headline and core consumer price inflation\* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and respective central banks. The favourable economic conditions were accompanied by substantial fund inflows, driving financial asset prices markedly higher in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Fund inflows into regional markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with gross portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose alongside the markets. Indeed, credit risk compensation in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

Hong Kong’s economy maintained robust growth momentum in the second half of 2017 amid buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The outlook for the Hong Kong economy remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while local inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. Hong Kong’s economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter on quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly in line with the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow robustly and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was robust on the back of favourable employment and income conditions, continued optimism in consumer sentiment and the positive wealth effect of rising asset prices. Despite weaker building and construction activities, higher business capital expenditure led to a notable increase in aggregate investment spending in the final quarter, following broadly stable performance over the preceding three quarters. Externally, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods remained a drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services contributed positively to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Sustained economic growth momentum led to an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment increased by around 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million, with the most notable increases recorded in the construction sector, the financing and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Externally, Hong Kong’s export performance will continue to benefit from the improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly due to favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. Regarding domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. While the improving economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, possible interest rate increases may have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3%–4% in 2018, while forecasts by international organisations and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment discussed in previous chapters, the performance of the Mainland Chinese economy amid tightening financial conditions, and developments in Hong Kong’s asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although sequential inflation momentum showed signs of picking up slightly in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index increased by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly in line with the average increase of around 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The recovery in fresh-letting private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures continued to remain moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labour costs and salary per capita As global inflation remains moderate and increases in domestic costs are steady, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 owing to the pass-through effect of rising fresh-letting private residential rentals. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 2.2% in 2018, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Despite the moderate inflation outlook, upside risks remain. Externally, a larger-than-expected increase in global inflation or commodity prices could add to local inflation momentum. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, falling below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the low interest rate environment after the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, Hong Kong households’ mortgage indebtedness increased. As US dollar interest rate normalisation progresses, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise in tandem with US dollar interest rates, correspondingly increasing households’ mortgage repayment burden and thereby weighing on household consumption. This box therefore examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to mortgage debt service payments (i.e. interest payments plus principal amortisation) as a share of income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution and income effects commonly discussed in economic theory, as well as the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices, when there is a mortgage repayment burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and hence households’ disposable income. This impact will increase with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans. In addition, principal amortisation varies with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, which also affects private consumption by changing households’ disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the outstanding mortgage debt servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the existing mortgage repayment burden indicator, which applies only to new mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the household sector, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the aggregate income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017 and the median ratio of mortgage payment and loan repayment to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population censuses. Both ratios trended downwards in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in aggregate household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997 and the substantial fall in mortgage rates over the same period. Despite a significant increase in property prices after the Global Financial Crisis, both ratios remained stable because the HKMA’s macroprudential measures on banks’ mortgage lending contained aggregate household mortgage leverage. In addition, longer tenors for new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payment and loan repayment to income We also compare the OMDSR with banks’ debt servicing ratio, which is the actual debt servicing-to-income ratio of applicants for new mortgages. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks’ debt servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As property prices were lower when existing mortgages were originated, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. banks’ debt servicing ratio). In addition, banks’ debt servicing ratio is higher because, in compliance with the HKMA’s prudential supervisory requirements, banks include repayments of non-mortgage loans when calculating the ratio. Following the Global Financial Crisis, both the OMDSR and banks’ debt servicing ratio remained stable, mainly because the HKMA’s prudential supervision of mortgage lending imposed a cap on banks’ debt servicing ratio, which also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks’ debt servicing ratio for new mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt burden indicators, but is more timely and can reflect the burden of all outstanding mortgage debt rather than only that of new mortgage debt. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the methodologies of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In the short-run specification, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we use real income (proxied by median household income and deflated by the CCPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, and deflated by the CCPI), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total loans continued to increase in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy continues to normalise. Fund-flow volatility may increase if global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate traded within a range of 7.799–7.827 against the US dollar (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened temporarily and stayed close to 7.80 between September and November 2017. This was mainly because increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end tightened liquidity conditions, thereby slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and prompting more unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for the US dollar increased, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Moving into 2018, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in an orderly manner despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, but the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index fluctuated mildly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index continued to closely track movements in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that equity portfolio investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents’ debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows in residents’ debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017 amid market optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that equity investment continued to record inflows despite the correction in global financial markets, while bond investment recorded mild outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalisation continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen and may lead to increased arbitrage activities. The possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should therefore not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalisation and rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board arrangements. Despite the US Fed’s interest rate hikes and continued balance-sheet reduction, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and more recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknotes (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged in the second half at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Within the total, the Aggregate Balance decreased, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills totalling HK$80 billion to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Moving into 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite the equity market correction. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply continued to grow in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In particular, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly because buoyant asset markets boosted investment demand. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by robust growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), but was partly offset by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its asset counterparts Foreign currency deposit growth, on the other hand, was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, growth in US dollar deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, after declining continuously for more than two years, other foreign currency deposits rebounded markedly by 8.4% in the second half. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in renminbi deposits. As growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with growth of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and three-month HIBORs increased by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, rising to monthly averages of 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December. The negative interest rate differentials between one- to three-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the ten-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield increased by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, the composite interest rate and the average lending rate for new mortgages Moving into 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. HIBORs declined in early January as year-end funding demand subsided. Thereafter, HIBORs remained broadly stable despite corrections in global and local equity markets. The overnight and three-month HIBORs closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. On the retail front, although banks’ lending rates rose alongside the surge in HIBORs, their funding costs generally remained low given the still-sizeable deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks’ average lending rate for new mortgages gradually increased by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in the one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, although the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, rose temporarily in October due to increased funding demand from initial public offerings, it remained soft for most of the second half and closed at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy continues to normalise and other major economies may also begin normalising interest rates. Meanwhile, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase fund-flow volatility. Nevertheless, the sizeable Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can provide a buffer against excessively rapid increases in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window will also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly in 2017 as a whole. Loan growth was as high as 10.2% in the first half before slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half amid favourable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. In particular, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly because of higher US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded robust growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong, including trade finance, slowed from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Growth in loans to the building and construction, and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half, partly because banks had been required to strengthen risk management for lending to property developers since June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and to the transport sector recorded only relatively modest growth, while loans to the wholesale and retail sector declined. By contrast, loan growth to financial and finance-related enterprises remained robust, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans by selected sector Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, accelerated further to 12.4% in the second half. The robust growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management customers secured by financial assets. Growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such secured loans were manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks on risk management for personal lending in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting limits on loan tenors and borrowers’ debt servicing ratios. On the other hand, despite increased residential transaction volumes, the average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages declined, and growth in residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio increased from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Retail banks’ profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016, mainly due to higher net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Credit growth moderated in the second half of 2017 after strong growth in the first half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a notable increase in HIBORs, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained low due to low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should stay vigilant against the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential fund outflows amid US monetary policy normalisation, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household indebtedness, banks should assess the potential impact of a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates on asset quality. To enhance banks’ resilience against system-wide risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a decrease in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, retail banks’ return on assets edged down to 1.15% in the second half of 2017 from 1.17% in the first half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence suggests that the improvement in the net interest margin was consistent with the increase in the average spread on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in Hong Kong’s syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans HIBORs increased across the board from September 2017, mainly driven by liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and from banks towards the year end, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, the three-month HIBOR reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up by 53 basis points from the end of June, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Moving into 2018, HIBORs appeared to stabilise as banks’ year-end liquidity demand eased. Despite the recent increase in HIBORs, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this background, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, stayed low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was observed in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars increased by 35 basis points, while their average deposit funding costs edged up by 12 basis points. Overall, the average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks increased by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve banks’ interest margins on HIBOR-based assets. However, this improvement may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information suggests that some banks have reduced the spread of their mortgage rates over benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Given the intense competition in the loan market, banks’ net interest margins may come under pressure if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above international minimum standards, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be well-capitalised. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper on proposed rules prescribing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions would benefit society by reducing the likelihood of financial crises, it would inevitably entail costs. Box 5 presents a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment suggests that implementing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose to 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 144.2% in the second quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions edged down to 49.4% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 49.7% in the second quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement is intended to reduce banks’ medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources for their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of not less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of December 2017, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged from six months earlier at 56.2% (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose to 82.7% at the end of December 2017 from 77.1% at the end of June (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at the end of December 2017 from 65.5% at the end of June. Overall, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 73.0% from 71.4% six months earlier. Banks should assess the implications of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, we estimate that the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would decline by an amount equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks Amid moderate but still favourable economic conditions, growth in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3% in the second half of 2017 from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half. Following two years of moderating growth, total loans grew robustly by 16.1% in 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks Strong credit growth is expected to continue as banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit growth. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2017 showed that 29% of the surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk associated with personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages fell further to 48.8% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 50.1% in the second quarter (Chart 5.12). This ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA introduced the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures in September 2009.

The global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened amid increased uncertainties arising from persistent trade tensions, tighter financial conditions and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The US Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that decisions would be “data dependent” and that “patience” was warranted, leading investors to rule out the possibility of further rate hikes. Nevertheless, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. In Hong Kong, despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU) by the Hong Kong dollar in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total loan growth moderated slightly in the second half of 2018, reflecting weaker credit demand amid headwinds from the ongoing China-US trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes falling markedly and housing prices declining, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds from increased uncertainties in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist for an extended period, they could significantly dampen business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact of a possible deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate exposures. The global economy continued to grow in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy grew solidly, growth momentum in other regions weakened. Among advanced economies, growth slowed in Japan and several major Euro area countries, while inflation remained low. Slowing global trade and a marked decline in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of weakening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively from its October 2018 projections. Amid a dimmer growth outlook and escalating trade tensions, global equity markets experienced sharp volatility towards the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, raising market concerns that the US was approaching a recession. Nevertheless, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term was low. That said, the global economic outlook remained fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation gave the Fed room to pause its rate hikes, the Fed’s data-dependent policy stance also suggested that financial markets might become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of the US-China and US-EU trade negotiations remained uncertain. In the UK, it remained unclear whether a solution to avoid a “hard Brexit” could be achieved. In East Asia, financial markets stabilised as the US dollar’s appreciation slowed and market expectations grew that the Fed would pause its rate hikes, but a deterioration in the external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade growth had already dragged on economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures had also subsided. Although this shift could ease the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks in supporting growth while containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector indebtedness in some regional economies remained severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia is that an unexpected shift in the Fed’s monetary policy could spill over to the sovereign debt markets of emerging market economies, including those in East Asia. In Mainland China, growth moderated further in the second half of 2018 amid increased uncertainties in the external environment and a slight slowdown in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remained uncertain as the China-US trade negotiations had yet to reach a conclusion. The marked contraction in shadow financing activities, which had increased financing difficulties for private enterprises, particularly small firms, over the past few quarters, together with weakening economic confidence, could also weigh on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers need to continue striking a balance between stabilising the economy and preventing and containing potential systemic risks by adopting accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted required reserve ratio cuts. Meanwhile, the authorities also introduced more supply-side measures to enhance productivity growth, such as promoting competition among firms of different ownership types, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered to a range of 6.0%–6.5% from around 6.5% in 2018. Risk-off sentiment dominated the Mainland financial markets in 2018. Banks’ asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage of listed non-financial corporates edged up. Nevertheless, banks’ loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, while their exposures to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline. Both developments helped protect the banking system against a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage of listed corporates in industries with excess capacity—one of the major sources of banks’ credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors contributing to the recent improvement in the business performance of industries with excess capacity. Economic activities in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018 compared with the first half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stagnated, while year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activities mainly reflected the direct or indirect drag of the China-US trade conflict on consumption and exports. The moderation in private consumption growth might have reflected increased economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect arising from the correction in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong’s merchandise export performance also deteriorated, especially after China and the US implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 takes a closer look at the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and discusses the near-term outlook and associated risks. Economic growth was expected to slow further in 2019, mainly due to weaker global economic growth. Amid the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance was expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption was expected to continue supporting economic growth amid a low unemployment rate and rising household income, but the outlook for aggregate investment spending could become more uncertain. The Government forecast real GDP growth for 2019 in the range of 2%–3%, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts averaged 2.3%. These forecasts were subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation partly reflected the earlier rise in fresh-letting rentals for local private residential properties. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years, total employment growth showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures were expected to remain moderate in 2019 as domestic growth momentum weakened. Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and traded within a range of 7.8062–7.8499 until the weak-side CU was triggered again four times in March 2019 (as at 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity. Moving into 2019, the Hong Kong dollar depreciated against the US dollar, partly due to the rebuilding of carry trade positions. Despite the renewed triggering of the weak-side CU in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. As the weak-side CU was triggered, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as at 19 March). Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally increased in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the three-month and 12-month HIBORs rose by around 30 basis points to monthly averages of 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December. Moving into 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined as seasonal demand faded. The composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding costs, increased from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. In view of rising funding costs, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in late September. At the end of January 2019, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.45% in tandem with the Best Lending Rates. With uncertainties surrounding China-US trade tensions and the Brexit negotiations persisting, fund flow volatility could intensify. In addition, the sizeable negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates could stimulate arbitrage activities and lead to fund outflows. Under such circumstances, fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side CU are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates had faced depreciation pressure amid market concerns over an escalation in China-US trade tensions. However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism arising from the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US. Despite the ongoing China-US trade tensions, funding conditions in the offshore interbank market had not been significantly affected so far. The overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% during the period. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite concerns over China-US trade tensions, Hong Kong’s CNH business was expected to continue expanding amid the opening of the Mainland’s capital account, the development of Stock Connect and Bond Connect, and regional economic co-operation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. The local equity market took a roller coaster ride over the past six months. In the early part of the review period, the market declined sharply amid continued US monetary policy tightening, significant differences between the two sides in the China-US trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in the Mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Fed shifted to a “patient” monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade war truce, China adopted further measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the US brought highly politicised legal charges against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides made conciliatory gestures, signalling their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this background, the local equity market rebounded sharply at the beginning of the year. Nevertheless, considerable uncertainties remained as the two sides discussed the details of any agreement, while future developments in the US federal government’s prosecution could complicate the situation, especially in the high-tech sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew modestly last year. Yields declined and market performance improved towards the end of the year as expectations of a slower pace of US monetary policy normalisation strengthened. As a result, bond fund flows reversed in the second half and recorded a modest increase. Issuance in Hong Kong’s CNH market rebounded sharply after declining for three consecutive years. However, as Mainland corporates continued to deleverage, total issuance remained lower than maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remained challenging, with its outlook hinging on global economic developments, particularly those in the Mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum weakened amid a confluence of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly outside the US. In view of the dimmer growth outlook, the US Federal Reserve (Fed) adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be “data dependent” and “patient”, and dropped its forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. With the Fed’s policy stance becoming data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data and perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened global trade policy uncertainty and geopolitical risks may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since late 2018 amid signs of a moderation in the US interest rate hiking cycle and a stabilising US dollar. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown due to a deteriorating external environment, namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weaker growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth momentum weakened further in the second half of 2018, while uncertainty surrounding the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Policymakers therefore introduced more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. In the face of these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and contain systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy. The global economy continued to expand broadly in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of moderation emerged. There were also clear signs of weakening growth momentum outside the US. A number of country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian government bond yields amid a fiscal standoff with the European Union, and social unrest in France, weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also created new challenges for commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for global growth in 2019 by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices of selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production in emerging market economies In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent a sharp correction amid weakening global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, market concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Fed’s indications that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, prompting concerns among some market participants that the US was approaching a recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Treasury yields and probability of a US recession Nevertheless, the likelihood of a US recession in the near term remains low. US economic fundamentals remain sound, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, and the likelihood of economic overheating prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy substantially is low. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began emphasising in early January that monetary policy would be data dependent, noting that subdued inflationary pressures allowed them to be “patient” in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the US Federal Open Market Committee dropped its forward guidance on further interest rate hikes and announced that it “would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments”. This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500 Index, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World ex USA Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Fed’s recent “dovish” signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain, depending on inflation and other developments. Subdued inflationary pressures thus far have given the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary policy normalisation. Stable inflation expectations in recent years support the case for being patient (Chart 2.5). In addition, as Fed Chairman Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slower growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainty. In view of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations However, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which generally signals higher inflation ahead (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that have essentially ruled out the possibility of a Fed rate hike in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the target range for the federal funds rate remaining unchanged versus at least one rate hike in 2019 In sum, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data dependent as a risk-management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the Euro area, the European Central Bank (ECB) ended its asset purchase programme in December while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, describing risks to the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside”. The implications of this downgrade to the ECB’s growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its latest policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary easing may be significant because its effectiveness has been questioned and the adverse effects of a prolonged ultra-low interest rate environment have become increasingly evident. For example, regional banks’ capital ratios declined from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from uncertainties surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, uncertain outcomes of forthcoming trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two other major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. In early December, the US Government announced that it would refrain from increasing tariffs on imports from China for 90 days and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the US and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. The uncertain outcomes of these trade negotiations may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the US, disagreements between the two parties over border security funding led to a 35-day Federal Government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be transitory, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives could lead to further policy gridlock. In the UK, risks associated with Brexit and its ramifications surged after the May Government’s Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and whether a last-minute solution can be devised to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit” remains uncertain. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the renewed US sanctions against Iran, could also create uncertainty over oil prices and thereby affect the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter after fluctuating during the first three quarters of last year. A stabilising US dollar since October and signs that the Fed would be patient regarding further interest rate hikes eased currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures on East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency index and fund flows Despite the stabilisation of financial markets, there are growing signs that the region may face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies, which reflect near-term external trade performance, have fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, signalling that near-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers’ Index new export orders indices for East Asian economies Against the backdrop of slowing growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline inflation and oil prices With recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar both remaining moderate, East Asian central banks face no imminent need to raise interest rates, easing the policy dilemma of balancing support for economic growth against containing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private-sector debt in some East Asian economies remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower private consumption growth and weaker export performance amid the China-US trade dispute. With global growth slowing, real GDP growth is also expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy and the performance of the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019, with the outlook subject to both upside and downside risks. Economic activities in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activities failed to sustain the strong momentum in the first half, with quarter-on-quarter GDP growth turning slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also moderated, with growth in the fourth quarter coming in below trend at 1.3%, dragging full-year growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Based on the seasonally adjusted expenditure-based GDP volume index. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component The weakening in economic activities was mainly attributable to the drag on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect effects of the China-US trade conflict. Private consumption growth moderated, possibly due to increased economic uncertainties and negative wealth effects arising from the correction in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Aggregate investment spending declined visibly amid fragile business confidence. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, especially after China and the US implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 takes a closer look at Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms Alongside the weakening in economic activities, employment growth appeared to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. Amid weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no signs of visible improvement. With global economic growth slowing further, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Given the challenging external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, while the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, private consumption growth is expected to moderate, partly reflecting weakened consumer confidence and the negative wealth effects arising from earlier corrections in asset prices. The outlook for fixed capital formation may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily alongside increased housing supply, firms may become more cautious about capital investment amid heightened economic uncertainties. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index continued to hover in contractionary territory, and forecasts of future economic growth based on the index point to a further moderation in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in the range of 2% to 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures continued to build up in recent months, they remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by increases in certain service prices. Earlier increases in fresh-letting private residential rentals and accelerated increases in the prices of meals out continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures remained generally moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Composite Consumer Price Index rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labour costs and per capita payroll Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019. This mainly reflects weakened domestic growth momentum. However, earlier increases in private residential rentals will continue to pass through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 2.2% for the year as a whole, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The inflation outlook above is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if the China-US trade frictions ease and the local economy performs better than expected, local inflation may be pushed up. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The China-US trade conflict intensified progressively in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the US imposed additional tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China respectively. Immediately following these two measures, Mainland China responded by imposing additional tariffs of 25% on an equivalent amount of US goods. The US escalated its measures further on 24 September by imposing additional tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing additional tariffs of 5%–10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. The two countries subsequently entered into negotiations to avoid further tariff hikes. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the additional tariffs would inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The China-US trade dispute therefore has important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook. Using more granular data, we also attempt to identify the traded goods directly affected by the additional tariffs in order to examine their impact more closely. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extract data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports affected by the respective rounds of additional tariffs described in the previous section. In the first two rounds, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods was broadened to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of additional tariffs as Lists 1, 2 and 3 respectively. After compiling these more granular trade data, we focus on year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. In addition, readers should exercise caution when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activities during that month were disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of the additional tariffs. Tariff-affected Hong Kong re-exports of Mainland origin Shortly after the additional tariffs were imposed, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US through Hong Kong appeared to have declined substantially or recorded slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, growth in re-exports of Lists 1 and 2 slowed in the first month after the additional tariffs were imposed, while re-exports of List 3 recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports of all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US through Hong Kong in 2018 Tariff-affected Hong Kong re-exports of US origin By contrast, goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports of List 1 appeared to have declined substantially in the months following the imposition of additional tariffs, but recovered towards the end of the year. Re-exports of List 2 generally recorded negative growth throughout the year, while growth in List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong in 2018 Front-loading Since there is sometimes a time lag between the announcement and actual implementation of tariffs (or simply due to the threat of additional tariffs), firms may increase shipments of affected goods ahead of the expected effective date of the tariffs. Indeed, some data and news reports suggest that such front-loading practices were fairly common. Some private-sector analysts also considered such practices to be one reason for the strong headline trade figures prior to the imposition of additional tariffs. More granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for goods on certain tariff lists, but this appeared to be confined to goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Growth in re-exports of Lists 1 and 2 increased in the months before their respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, growth in re-exports from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong (Chart B3.2) showed no clear signs of front-loading by firms. Hong Kong re-exports unaffected by additional tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the additional tariffs accounted for only around 4%–5% of the total value of Hong Kong’s re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs should also be examined. We find that re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in the final two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Moreover, the decline in growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) was visibly larger from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slower growth in re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs partly reflected a broader weakening in external demand. As the continued trade frictions heightened uncertainty, global financial conditions tightened and geopolitical risks increased, external demand may come under broader pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activities, as reflected in corrections in major equity markets. Import demand from other economies was consequently dampened, restraining Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong’s re-exports in 2018 Even if the China-US trade frictions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remains challenging. The likely slowdown in global growth in 2019 (see Chapter 2) is bound to restrain Hong Kong’s export performance further. Various business sentiment indicators show that firms of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trading sector particularly subdued. Other trade-related sectors such as logistics may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Business outlook survey of Hong Kong’s import and export sector

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity driven by expectations of seasonal funding demand. Moving into 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly because corporates repatriated funds raised through IPOs and the market rebuilt carry trade positions, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU) was triggered in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before declining in January 2019. Looking ahead, uncertainties arising from the ongoing US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation may lead to greater volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, carry trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side CU again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side CU was triggered again four times in March 2019 (up to 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, but then gradually declined in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity, leading to the unwinding of carry trades. Moving into 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates’ repatriation of funds raised through IPOs and the market’s rebuilding of carry trade positions. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken gradually and triggering the weak-side CU again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side CU, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance had remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), before declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side CU in March (as at 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar funds that had flowed out since April 2018 represented only a small fraction of the approximately HK$1 trillion that had flowed in since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Indicators of fund flows Broadly tracking the movements of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and thus had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER generally followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER The latest balance of payments statistics show that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased equity market volatility, outflows of local residents’ equity securities investment accelerated, more than offsetting inflows of non-residents’ portfolio investment in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, uncertainties arising from the ongoing US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation may heighten fund-flow volatility. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to fund outflows. Under the LERS, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and the weak-side CU may be triggered again. Fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side CU are part of the normal operation of the LERS. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation process and the repeated triggering of the weak-side CU from April to August, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year to HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base mainly reflected the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no notable change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side CU in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as at 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for broader measures of the Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) increased by 3.6% in the first half of the year, but grew only slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits were little changed compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6).
