Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly owing to fewer investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to register strong growth as deposit interest rates increased. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that changes in banks’ capital and reserves (included under “net other items”) slowed the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3. Chart 4.5 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its asset counterparts Foreign currency deposit growth accelerated in the second half of the year. As banks attracted more deposits after raising preferential US dollar deposit rates, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half and became the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits grew slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) grew modestly by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Despite the still sizeable Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposits, HIBORs began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank interest rates, making them more volatile than longer-term interbank interest rates (Chart 4.7). The three-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, around 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Moving into 2019, HIBORs generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The average three-month and 12-month HIBORs fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, the yields on three-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds declined by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate increased from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before declining to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of rising funding costs, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September. However, retail banks did not adjust their Best Lending Rates again after the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised further in December. Meanwhile, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose in tandem with the Best Lending Rates to around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, movements in US dollar interest rates, fund flows and local financial market activities, such as IPO subscription activities, will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains sizeable and the banking system holds a large amount of Exchange Fund Bills, which banks can use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating US-China trade tensions, both the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi depreciated against the US dollar from the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates So far, the ongoing US-China trade tensions have not had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally because of seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before declining to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting the monetary easing measures recently introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of developments in the US-China trade talks on liquidity in the CNH interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, outstanding CDs declined further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly owing to reduced CD issuance and a relatively large amount of CDs maturing in October.

Retail banks’ profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017, mainly due to higher net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank rates and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, the overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks increased notably, but remained at a low level. Amid uncertainties in the external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilising from November onwards, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from lingering uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations, a slowdown in the global economy, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant against the impact of a possible further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate exposures. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets rose to 1.23% from 1.14% (Chart 5.1). The strong performance was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income, which more than offset the increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose to 1.27% from 1.16% in 2017. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong dollar interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period, as banks generally raised time deposit rates to compete for long-term stable funding. In addition, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Reflecting both higher wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) increased from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained low by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued on an upward trend. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs increased by 36 basis points, following a 40-basis-point increase in the first half of the year (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and tenor of licensed banks The cumulative increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in the overall funding costs of Hong Kong banks. This might have a positive impact on retail banks’ HIBOR-based mortgage loans, which the industry had actively promoted over the preceding few years. However, further improvement in the net interest margin might become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans had reached their Best Lending Rate-based interest rate caps. Given the uncertainty over the timing of future increases in Best Lending Rates, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation might weigh on the overall net interest margin. Looking ahead, heightened uncertainties in the external environment may cloud banks’ profitability outlook. In particular, against the background of slowing global economic growth, lingering uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this leads to a significant decline in lending and deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks’ profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions increased further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated basis. 2. With effect from 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based Leverage Ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum Leverage Ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions increased from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated stable funding positions of authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand a range of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2018, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions edged up to 55.7% from 54.5% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities comprise negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at the end of the year (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions declined from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. By contrast, as growth in Hong Kong dollar deposits was significantly slower than that in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at the end of the year. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions was estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks 1. The interest rate shock refers to a standardised 200-basis-point parallel interest rate shock to institutions’ interest rate risk exposures. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to its impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. Against the background of lingering uncertainties surrounding the China-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed notably in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilising from November 2018 onwards. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Growth in domestic loans slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, growth in total loans slowed markedly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the near term. According to the HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2018, 82% of all surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged in the next three months, while the share expecting demand to decrease rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite the slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio declined slightly to 0.50%, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks 1. Classified loans are those loans graded as “substandard”, “doubtful” or “loss”. 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of the Hong Kong offices and overseas branches of retail banks. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include retail banks’ major overseas subsidiaries. On a half-yearly basis, growth in personal loans slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to slower growth in private loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, which offset the faster growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal GDP grew more slowly than personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak since early 2020 has dealt simultaneous shocks to both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic shock from the outbreak, financial markets have remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthening, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable and total deposits increasing modestly, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After rebounding modestly in the first half of 2019, total loan growth moderated in the second half. The residential property market generally softened, albeit with some fluctuations, from mid-2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should carefully assess the potential impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios if these risk factors intensify. Global economic growth had shown tentative signs of stabilisation since the fourth quarter of 2019, supported by greater monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of US-China trade tensions and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit”. However, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide since late January has raised market concerns and triggered sharp volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks posed by the outbreak, several major central banks have substantially reduced interest rates and expanded their liquidity facilities, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions have tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp declines in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will weigh on global economic activity, with the magnitude of the economic impact depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, tensions between the US and its major trading partners may re-emerge, while the UK’s post-Brexit trade negotiations with the European Union may also prove difficult. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 The region’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region have recently reported revenue growth, but it remains to be seen whether there will be a broad-based recovery in the tech cycle. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China announced in December 2019, with the trade truce reducing global trade uncertainties to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by a number of regional economies may weigh on Asia’s tourism industry, particularly in economies that are more dependent on exports of tourism services. Given the region’s close supply-chain linkages with Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China should temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures remain in view of the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made economic stabilisation a priority for 2020, while also emphasising the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts suggest that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed to a possible decline in the equity of private industrial enterprises in recent years, which has been regarded as a sign of “private-sector retreat”. Box 2 examines the factors driving changes in the equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using data on listed companies in 2018, and finds that private or small enterprises are not intrinsically more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. While negative earnings were found to be the most significant driver, other factors, particularly structural factors, also warrant attention (see Box 2 for details). Hong Kong’s economic activity contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weaker domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main drag on GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely disrupted consumption activities and weakened the economic outlook, thereby undermining consumer and business confidence. Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained sluggish amid a renewed escalation of US-China trade tensions, slowing global economic growth and a severe downturn in inbound tourism. In view of the severe headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks more room to step up their support for the domestic economy and help moderate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion–HK$300 billion to businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent outbreak also posing significant downside risks. As the retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism and transport sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, the package of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020–21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and special low-interest loans to businesses with a 100% Government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.2 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, giving banks more room to step up their support for the domestic economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure from the outbreak. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak amid fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China is expected to have a modest positive impact on the domestic economy in the near term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-boundary economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, US-China trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising and the real wage index falling year on year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the coronavirus outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate will rise further in view of the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 provides a more detailed discussion of recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up into the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to higher prices of fresh pork; inflation momentum subsequently moderated gradually as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to ease in the near term amid weak economic conditions, consolidating private residential rentals and moderate imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2020 to range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for Hong Kong dollars, including that arising from initial public offerings (IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually from mid-October 2019. Moving into December, the strengthening momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate increased further, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly because tighter liquidity towards the year-end prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner during the review period, without triggering the Convertibility Undertakings. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have fluctuated since the fourth quarter of 2019, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 examines how market interest in forthcoming IPO activities affects the three-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the Composite Interest Rate rose gradually from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. With some banks raising the interest rate cap linked to the Best Lending Rate, the average lending rate for new mortgages increased to around 2.6% in October, but edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020 following reductions in market Best Lending Rates from November. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthening, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable and total deposits increasing modestly, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. Nevertheless, the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus outbreak amid uncertainties in the external environment needs to be monitored. With its ample foreign reserves and robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. During the review period, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened on market expectations of a US-China trade agreement, but came under weakening pressure following the coronavirus outbreak from late January 2020. The offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi in the latter part of 2019. Its discount widened briefly at the end of January 2020, although the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a modest decline in the previous review period. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion at the end of January 2020. Hong Kong’s other renminbi businesses also expanded, with strong growth in renminbi bank lending and renminbi trade settlement business. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system stayed high at RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased allocation to renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising hopes of a global economic recovery. However, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide since late January 2020 dashed hopes of a recovery and heightened investor concerns about a global recession, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments introduced stimulus measures from early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 clouded the outlook for regional economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector being particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia also continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and elevated private-sector leverage. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US should temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, although the authorities’ monetary and fiscal policy responses should provide some buffer. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth continued to lack momentum in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, growth showed tentative signs of stabilisation at the beginning of the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly supported by the earlier policy easing by the US Fed and the ECB, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US “Phase One” trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Indices However, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide since late January and the ensuing economic disruptions raised market concerns and triggered a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities and the resulting drag on economic growth in the Mainland will generate significant spillover effects that could reverberate globally (Chart 2.3). The surge in coronavirus infections outside Mainland China since late February could further intensify supply-chain disruptions and poses a risk of directly weighing on local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and option-adjusted spread of the Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, some central banks, including the US Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, cut interest rates from early March, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nevertheless, financial markets remained under immense selling pressure, resulting in a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which could in turn exacerbate downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for advanced economies Apart from developments in the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations could be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are unlikely to proceed smoothly, prolonging post-Brexit uncertainty. In addition, the sharp fall in oil prices since March will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 amid subdued global demand. East Asia’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there were tentative signs that the regional tech down cycle was bottoming out, including reports of improved earnings at the end of 2019 by major regional electronics companies,6 it remains to be seen whether regional technology exports will stage a meaningful rebound. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainty also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region’s potential economic growth over the longer term. To support economic growth amid moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea further lowered their policy rates in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also reduced its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak raised concerns that regional economies could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As many economies in the region imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism sector was the first to bear the brunt, with economies more reliant on visitors from Mainland China and tourism service exports being more severely affected by the outbreak (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and worsening epidemic would also disrupt regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese visitors In the near term, the epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Judging from the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these effects may be transitory, although the actual outcome will depend on the severity and geographical spread of the epidemic and the effectiveness of government actions to contain it. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although corporate earnings are expected to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), loose global monetary conditions have encouraged the search for yield, pushing up asset prices without support from fundamentals. As a result, regional equity markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituents of benchmark equity indices Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth could make it more difficult for the region’s private sector to service its debt. While lower domestic interest rates could provide some breathing space for indebted firms and households, they could also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector could be exacerbated as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, although this effect may be confined to firms with stronger financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, on the external front, East Asian economies may face greater risks from an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite the recent progress made under the China-US Phase One trade agreement, trade tensions between China and the US persist as the fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain unresolved. The growing trade surpluses of many regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations may continue to seek more sourcing channels outside China-centred supply chains to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies excluding China with the US had increased to around US$167 billion. If their trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the Asian economies concerned could become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US Government imposed steep tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surpluses with the US Over the past decade, increasing integration of international financial markets has led to a significant rise in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices, commonly known as passive funds, but also actively managed funds that use investment indices as benchmarks.9 By bringing in overseas investors that the economies concerned would otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Such funds therefore enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor bases, supporting the long-term growth and stability of their markets. But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? For passive bond funds, there are concerns that their investments could weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby resulting in elevated corporate leverage.10 In addition, it has been argued that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has increased the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, rendering emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, more vulnerable.11 This box assesses the financial stability implications of index-driven investment in relation to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to constituent bonds according to the weights of those bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds may reduce the incentives for issuers of constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour could encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage has risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of firms in individual emerging market economies in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for passive bond fund investment in their bonds,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term, rather than short-term, leverage of the corporate issuers concerned. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated effects. Apart from promoting the development of corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the expanded base of long-term bond investors brought about by passive bond funds also supports the development of emerging market corporates. We also find that the above effect is significant only for emerging market corporates with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with greater debt servicing ability and lower leverage (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged firms or those with weaker debt servicing ability appear less likely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. Overall, the above findings suggest that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase solvency risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Hong Kong’s economy contracted in the second half of 2019 amid weakening private consumption, reduced investment spending and poor export performance, entering recession for the first time since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent coronavirus outbreak also posing significant downside risks. The economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. Hong Kong’s economy contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, contrasting with the 2.9% growth in 2018 and marking the first annual contraction since the Global Financial Crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities slowed visibly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP declined successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main drag on GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely disrupted consumption activities, while the resulting deterioration in the economic outlook dampened consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract visibly from the third quarter onwards. 33 Aggregate investment spending remained weak and weighed on GDP in the fourth quarter amid increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment. 34 Externally, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained sluggish amid escalating China-US trade tensions, weakening global economic growth and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Chart 3.2). 35 Amid a sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports weighed on GDP in the third quarter but contributed positively to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Given the severe headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to ease the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment and support enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and hard-hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport and tourism. 36 To provide banks with greater scope to step up support for the local economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion–HK$300 billion to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong’s economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent outbreak also posing significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020-21 Budget could provide relief to households and enterprises, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to enterprises with a 100% Government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 The HKMA’s further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will provide banks with greater scope to step up support for the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure as a result of the outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak amid fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued following the completion of some major infrastructure projects. On the external front, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the near term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-boundary economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the growth forecasts by international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in previous chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and increased further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). In particular, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment declined by 0.5% year on year in the second half of 2019 and continued to fall to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly seen in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year on year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges and the unemployment rate is highly likely to rise further. Box 3 discusses in greater detail recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices, before inflation momentum gradually eased as economic activities weakened. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying CCPI increased by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the rate of increase moderating slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also softened from a peak of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The easing in inflation momentum reflected reduced price pressures across a number of CPI components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained visible because of rising fresh pork prices, while price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. For services, growth in the CPI rental component also trended down as the growth of fresh-letting private residential rentals had slowed earlier (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labour costs Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. With private residential rentals continuing to moderate, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate amid weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation for 2020 in the range of 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying and headline inflation rates of 2.5% and 1.7% respectively. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe-than-expected economic deterioration, for example due to a prolonged coronavirus outbreak, could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, more severe disruptions to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the visible slowdown in the local economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents continued that the unemployment rate rose more visibly to 3.3% at the end of 2019. The labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020 as a result of the coronavirus outbreak. Against this background, this box analyses recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook, including why the overall labour market remained broadly resilient during the first three quarters of 2019, with the unemployment rate showing little change, and the implications for future developments. It also examines several risk factors that could lead to a sharp increase in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand involves costs. Indeed, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature may explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% even when real economic activities deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth and unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade and retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors continued to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, while financial activities relating to fintech development and initial public offerings were also highly active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. Moreover, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appeared to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of the public administration, social and personal services sectors to the economic cycle is more neutral. In other words, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors even during an economic slowdown. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate 40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 Meanwhile, the increase in employment during the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted visibly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment declined during the recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some changes in the structure of the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the rising share of voluntary part-time employees may have helped firms retain staff. Indeed, the shares of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in total employment (about 7% in 2017). 42 Firms may therefore retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time staff. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the increased share of part-time workers in the employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October, with the upward momentum gaining further traction in December and keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar partly arose from equity-related demand and partly from the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions amid tighter liquidity towards the year end. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Although volatility in fund flows may increase if the coronavirus outbreak affects market sentiment amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong is capable of withstanding fund outflow pressures without compromising its financial stability, given its ample foreign reserves and robust banking system. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including that arising from initial public offerings (IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Moving into December, its upward momentum gained further traction, with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate staying on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone from mid-December to February. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate partly reflected buoyant IPO activities and partly the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions amid tighter liquidity towards the year end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) Broadly tracking the movements of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and thus had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER generally followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER When measuring fund flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows and are useful for assessing monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through the Hong Kong banking system and are useful for assessing the stability of Hong Kong’s overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decline. As the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged since April 2019 and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong are a useful indicator. If there are substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will necessarily decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no notable cross-border fund outflows. Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained limited. Nevertheless, the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak need to be closely monitored. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the domestic economy, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, increasing by 4.0% from end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base The broad Hong Kong dollar money supply remained broadly stable during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and then edged up by 0.2% in the seven months since end-June 2019. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since end-June mainly reflected increases in banks’ net foreign currency assets and the Monetary Base, with the latter driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). Hong Kong dollar deposits, the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, remained broadly unchanged in the seven months since end-June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its asset counterparts Foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% in the seven months since end-June 2019 (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decrease in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) grew steadily by 1.2% from end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s total broad money supply also grew at a relatively stable pace, with total M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively from end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be volatile due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business- and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, amid buoyant IPO activities in the Hong Kong equity market, the overnight HIBOR experienced greater volatility in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 Other short-term HIBORs generally increased during the review period. Subscriptions for large IPOs exert significant pressure on overnight rates. The empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to upcoming IPO activities also affects the three-month HIBOR. This may occur if market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large IPOs and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downwards in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield of the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond declined by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield of the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond decreased by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages On the retail front, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. The increase mainly reflected banks’ continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, resulting in an increase in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following a reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate, several retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans, for HIBOR-based mortgages, major banks raised the interest rate cap linked to the Best Lending Rate, causing the average lending rate for new mortgages to rise to around 2.63% in October. 45 Following the reduction in Best Lending Rates in the market from November, the average mortgage rate edged down to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks to US economic activity posed by the coronavirus outbreak and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March and 15 March (US time). While HIBORs track movements in US dollar interest rates over the longer term, short-term HIBORs may be affected by local factors that influence demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as local IPO activities. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, HIBORs may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funding. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet banks’ interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightness, banks may make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid concerns over a possible escalation in the China-US trade conflict, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened notably in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Moving into October, market expectations of a resumption of China-US trade negotiations reversed the renminbi’s depreciation trend. The offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly rose beyond 6.9 in mid-January 2020 after China and the US signed the Phase One trade agreement. However, since the end of January, both the offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced weakening pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, but generally traded at a premium later in 2019. The discount widened briefly at the end of January 2020, although the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month offshore renminbi HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to MSCI’s A-share adjustments, and around the Lunar New Year holiday at the end of January 2020.

Amid increased uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined slightly in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although total loan growth moderated in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the review period. Accordingly, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions increased. However, given the stable level of the Aggregate Balance of the banking system and broadly stable deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increase in corporate leverage and household indebtedness, banks should carefully assess the impacts on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit59 of retail banks decreased slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, compared with 1.23% in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), retail banks’ net interest income continued to register moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in retail banks’ loan impairment charges and operating expenses led to a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three 25-basis-point cuts in the US Federal Funds Target Rate in the second half of 2019, significant downward pressure has yet to emerge in the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market. Instead, affected by several domestic factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, longer-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (the blue line in Chart 5.3). On the retail front, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) gradually increased from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained low by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in the US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates, supporting banking sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and maturity have been calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and domestic environments will continue to cloud banks’ profitability outlook. These factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could weaken the already subdued momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread monetary easing by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, potentially putting pressure on banks’ net interest margins in the period ahead. Domestically, the local social incidents since mid-2019 continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies in the period ahead, the outlook for credit demand and banks’ asset quality may deteriorate. In terms of overall market developments, following the granting of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector began rolling out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market shares by launching more convenient products and offering more attractive deposit rates to acquire new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the near-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks’ operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results of Box 5 show that the extent of financial technology adoption by banks in Hong Kong is statistically associated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. At the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions increased further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratios, the Basel III non-risk-based Leverage Ratio requirement serves to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio65 requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions increased from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio,66 one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated stable funding positions among authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand various liquidity shocks. At the end of 2019, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11).
