The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hope of economic reopening and boosted the global growth outlook. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary accommodation, financial markets repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remained clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery was expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels and lasting economic scarring from the pandemic would pose challenges to policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU), mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of sizeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activities and subdued credit demand amid recurring outbreaks of the pandemic, total loans of the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, but still recorded a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and lingering geopolitical risks would continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic could weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant against the impact of the relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again from the fourth quarter as COVID-19 infections resurged. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development towards the end of 2020, markets expected that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, facilitating the normalisation of the global economy and an acceleration in growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary accommodation, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties would continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remained to be seen whether vaccines could be distributed widely. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive policy easing could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to withdraw monetary accommodation earlier and bringing an end to financial markets’ expectations of a “lower for longer” monetary policy environment. Over the longer term, policymakers would need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scarring. In East Asia, GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio inflows into the region rebounded and the search for yield re-emerged. Notwithstanding these positive developments, East Asia continued to face lingering uncertainties arising from the pandemic. First, in the global race to procure vaccines, the region’s less developed economies might lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and services sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage or effectiveness, coupled with weakened fiscal positions of governments in the region, could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook would still depend heavily on developments in the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts projected the Mainland economy to grow by 8.4% in 2021. After depreciating for several months in early 2020, the renminbi strengthened for the remainder of the year amid an accelerating economic recovery, a weaker US dollar and strong inflows into the Mainland bond market. A detailed study showed that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Box 1 for details). Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained far below its pre-pandemic level. Amid a modest pickup in domestic demand and a further expansion in merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed visibly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first-ever decline for two consecutive years. The latest sectoral GDP data showed that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more sharply than the overall economy amid the pandemic. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist pandemic-hit sectors and members of the public, and to enhance Hong Kong’s anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for the unemployed. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, as well as an extension of the repayment period for trade finance facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines offering hope that economic activities could return to normal, the local economy was expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole, but the strength and pace of the recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including developments in the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support to Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecast real GDP growth of 3.5%–5.5% in 2021, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure amid weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The year-on-year underlying consumer price inflation rate declined markedly to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also remained low despite some fluctuations in recent months. Given the continued challenging global and domestic economic conditions, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressures would likely remain mild in the near term. In particular, the earlier moderation in fresh-letting private residential rentals would continue to contain domestic inflation. The market consensus forecast headline inflation of a moderate 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecast underlying and headline inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side CU, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fund-raising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side. During the review period, the strong-side CU was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side CU was triggered 85 times, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. An analysis by geographical location showed that total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of sizeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties relating to developments in the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions might heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong had ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and was therefore capable of withstanding such volatility. As the triggering of the strong-side CU increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. As funding costs declined, the average lending rate for new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Alongside the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY), the offshore renminbi (CNH) had appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. During most of the review period, the CNH traded at a premium to the CNY, with the average premium in the fourth quarter at around 100 pips, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, Hong Kong’s renminbi bank lending declined while renminbi trade settlement increased, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system stayed high at RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-boundary fund-flow channels connecting to the Mainland. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to benefit from the continuing opening of the Mainland’s capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by rising global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through the Southbound Stock Connect, the local equity market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose amid the unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies, optimism over positive progress in vaccine development that could help accelerate the recovery in economic activities, and reduced global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses following the sharp decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and briefly surpassing the 31,000 level in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi debt markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded as market confidence recovered rapidly amid the unprecedented economic stimulus measures introduced by governments around the world. Despite a moderate rebound in bond yields over the same period, bond yields globally, including those in Hong Kong, continued to hover near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development raising hopes that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually end and global economic growth could accelerate, coupled with expectations of a “low-for-longer” global monetary policy stance, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the disconnect between buoyant financial market expectations and the still-challenging macroeconomic environment could lead to asset price volatility if the economic recovery proves weaker than expected or policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, because of higher-than-expected inflation). Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support and how to address the many legacies of the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-term economic scarring. Lingering uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continued to cloud the economic recovery in East Asia, with less-developed emerging market economies in the region potentially facing greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in vaccination programmes could reverse the prevailing optimism and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the economic recovery gathered pace in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remains highly uncertain and will depend largely on the evolution of the pandemic and China-US tensions. The Government therefore announced that it would maintain its supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of containing systemic risks. Benefiting from the release of pent-up purchasing power following economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, the renewed rise in COVID-19 infections since the fourth quarter prompted governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, weakening global growth momentum again. The emergence of more transmissible variants at the end of 2020 and their subsequent spread across the world further aggravated the situation. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use at the end of 2020 raised hopes that the pandemic would eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normal and growth to accelerate. Another impetus supporting the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus, including major central banks’ commitments to “low-for-longer” monetary policies amid subdued inflation and continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised up its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF forecasts of real GDP growth in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, growing market optimism and rising share prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from an economic recovery drove global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major equity indices However, the disconnect between robust financial market performance and the still-challenging macroeconomic environment could result in asset market volatility in the face of multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control hinges on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Despite global mechanisms such as COVAX to promote more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supplies mean that low vaccination rates are likely to pose a more acute problem for lower-income emerging market economies. If the pandemic is not brought under control as expected, social distancing and other restrictions may need to remain in place, thereby undermining the prospects for a global recovery. Chart 2.3 Share of population having received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the financial market rally has been built on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the “low-for-longer” monetary policy stance. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen amid the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, robust monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary accommodation, while higher-than-expected inflation data could also increase financial market volatility. Chart 2.4 US and Euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, significant uncertainty surrounds the future of China-US relations. The trend towards China-US “decoupling”, particularly in the financial and technological spheres, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance towards Mainland China across both US political parties, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger financial market turbulence in the period ahead. Looking ahead, policymakers will have to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. While premature withdrawal could jeopardise the economic recovery and result in “cliff effects”, these measures are costly over the longer term, creating fiscal burdens and delaying the post-pandemic reallocation of resources that will be necessary, for example, by allowing “zombie firms” with no longer viable business models to survive through continued government support. Policymakers will also have to address the many legacies of the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 as corporate revenues declined and government spending surged (Chart 2.5). Although the problems arising from the rapid increase in debt may not be imminent given the currently extremely low level of global interest rates, continued debt accumulation by the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy concerns the potential long-term economic losses or scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty may cause firms to reduce investment, while workers suffering from prolonged unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after plunging in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was mainly driven by a rebound in exports, with demand particularly strong for exports of electronics and technological equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face customer contact, continued to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite lingering uncertainty surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment flows resumed. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond fund inflows amid improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced-economy bonds (Chart 2.7). Equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020 as signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were launched. Regional currencies appreciated correspondingly amid portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg-JP Morgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by around 10% from its low in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows East Asia continued to face lingering uncertainties surrounding the pandemic. First, while vaccine rollouts offered hope to the region’s hardest-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early access to vaccines raised procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also posed challenges to the region’s logistics and public health capabilities. As a result, less-developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, while uneven vaccination across economies may prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related sectors. Second, as investor optimism has been driven largely by vaccine rollouts, substantially weaker-than-expected progress or effectiveness of vaccination could bring the prevailing capital inflows and rally in financial asset prices to an end. An abrupt decline in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports continued to grow on strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-tech products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, Mainland GDP still grew by 2.3% despite the unprecedented shock from the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution to GDP growth by demand component Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts project robust growth of 8.4% in the Mainland economy in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained will still depend partly on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have normalised, service sectors continued to experience some disruption following renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. Externally, despite a return to export growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remained uncertain amid new waves of infections in most advanced economies. In addition, China-US tensions may not ease in the near term, although the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the agreed Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the EU could help further integrate China with other economies and partly offset the adverse impact of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. In view of the continued uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, the Government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that there would be no major change in the prevailing policy stance in 2021 in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of containing systemic risks, such as maintaining stable macro leverage and ensuring the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan prioritises technological self-reliance and the dual-circulation strategy, with the aim of raising per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on bond issuers’ repayment capacity appeared limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of bond defaults increased in 2020 because of a sharp rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises (Chart 2.9). While the increase in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflected the Central Government’s determination to break the “implicit guarantee” for state-owned enterprises in order to promote more rational market pricing of risks, constrained fiscal space among some local governments, particularly those in less-developed regions, may also have been a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Amount and ratio of onshore bond defaults Corporate issuers’ financing costs increased in the second half of 2020, particularly for some higher-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to higher financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a notable widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields In the property market, housing prices in the Mainland continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing price growth was much slower in lower-tier cities (Chart 2.11). The housing oversupply that had plagued third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below its peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level, Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand revived and exports of goods expanded further. With COVID-19 vaccination offering hope of a return to normal economic activities, the local economy is expected to resume growth in 2021 after recording its sharpest contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressures should stay mild. Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), although economic activities remained well below their pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first two consecutive years of contraction in history. The latest data on GDP by economic activity also show that economic activities in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover in the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Domestic private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, although consumer sentiment remained weak as social distancing measures were reimposed amid the third and fourth waves of the local epidemic. Aggregate investment spending also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment briefly improved. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance, particularly exports to Mainland China, Hong Kong’s trade in goods expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism was still at a standstill. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged on GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower recovery in exports of goods than in imports. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to support the economy, including the provision of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for the unemployed. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines offering hope of a return to normal economic activities, Hong Kong’s economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong’s trade in goods and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for the whole of 2021 in the range of 3.5%–5.5%, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021 (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS epidemic. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed a continued decline in the number of job vacancies. The nominal index of payroll per person engaged, which reflects labour earnings, saw its growth slow to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure given weak economic conditions. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell markedly year on year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also remained low despite some fluctuations in recent months. Specifically, price pressures on basic food eased, while the cost of meals out declined visibly, reflecting the provision of more takeaway discounts by restaurants while dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other tradable goods, such as durable goods, remained moderate. On the services front, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained weak as private residential rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6).
