In particular, local inflation will continue to be restrained by the earlier slowdown in fresh-letting private residential rental growth. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying and headline inflation rates of 1% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. As inbound tourism rapidly fell into a slump amid the ravages of the COVID-19 pandemic, there have been concerns that the crisis may have a scarring effect on the subsequent labour market recovery. Against this background, this box empirically analyses the impact of a tourism boom on Hong Kong’s labour market to shed light on the potential implications of the current tourism slump. Inbound tourism has experienced dramatic rises and falls since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the outbreak of SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) in 2003. Visitor arrivals began to surge after the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply individually to visit Hong Kong once or twice a year, with each stay lasting no more than seven days. The IVS was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry IVS endorsements permitting multiple visits to Hong Kong within one year. Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure links with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, while inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Taking the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We regard the introduction of the IVS in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock because its timing was nearly exogenous and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. The main data for our analysis are population data from Hong Kong’s Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Census or By-census. We also define the tourism-related sectors as the catering, retail, hotel and transport sectors. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers aged 20–40 in the “treatment group” and older workers aged 41–65 in the “comparison group”. We assign the younger cohort to the “treatment group” because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the labour market impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS may change over time, we also employ an event study to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers, particularly women and those with only secondary education, were more likely to enter tourism-related sectors after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the impact of the IVS on the probability of younger women working in tourism-related sectors was especially significant and persistent, remaining close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards in terms of the average difference in the probability of entering such sectors relative to the older cohort (Chart B2.2). Using a similar approach, we also compare the income of workers in tourism-related sectors (the treatment group) with that of workers in non-tourism-related sectors (the comparison group). The estimation results show that, after the implementation of the IVS, income growth among workers in tourism-related sectors was higher than that among employees in non-tourism-related sectors. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other sectors, female workers and workers with lower educational attainment in tourism-related sectors experienced higher and increasing income gains of 3–20 percentage points (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the income of female workers and workers with lower educational attainment The above results are broadly in line with international experience, showing that tourism is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In Hong Kong’s case, our findings are also consistent with previous analysis that strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism has fallen from boom to bust, these groups of workers may be more severely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU), which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities and southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) declined across the board. Although uncertainties surrounding the development of the coronavirus pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and lingering China-US tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is capable of withstanding the pressures arising from fund-flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side CU, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant IPO activities and southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects (Chart 4.1). Although some of the proceeds raised through IPOs were remitted out of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505–7.7544 in November and December amid improved sentiment in the local equity market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards the year-end. With fundraising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the Aggregate Balance increased as the strong-side CU was triggered multiple times, reflecting substantial inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side CU was triggered 47 times between September and October 2020. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CU was triggered 85 times in total during 2020, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits suggested that there was no sign of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual fund movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) declined, broadly tracking the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and lingering China-US tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities, such as IPOs, resulting in substantial fund inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, such fundraising activities may attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. With ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, Hong Kong is capable of withstanding fund-flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% in the eight months since end-June 2020 (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the multiple triggering of the strong-side CU. Meanwhile, the other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities increased Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans. As a result, Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component rose markedly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the completion of IPO activities and the repayment of IPO subscription loans by customers, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Moving into January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 rose sharply again, mainly driven by a large-scale IPO at the end of January. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased by 21.7% in the seven-month period since end-June. Excluding the impact of the IPO activity at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased moderately by 9.1%. Analysed by counterpart assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the increase in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the expansion of the Monetary Base following the triggering of the strong-side CU (Chart 4.7). As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 22.9% over the same period. Excluding the impact of the IPO activity at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined amid low deposit rates, the decrease was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% in the seven-month period since end-June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while deposits in other foreign currencies grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits with AIs rose markedly by 13.2% during the review period amid short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO activity at the end of January, total deposits increased moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, HIBORs generally stayed at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not experience significant fluctuations owing to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Broadly tracking the US dollar yield curve, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields increasing (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level generally followed the decline in HIBORs. The composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, declined further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Amid lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the one-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the LERS, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the US, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should remain low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting Mainland China’s more favourable economic outlook relative to the rest of the world and the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell’s announcement at the end of September that Mainland government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index provided further support to the strengthening of the renminbi through investment demand. During most of the review period, the CNH traded at a premium to the CNY, averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, it mostly traded below 4% (Chart 4.11). The three-month CNH HIBOR declined in late December, tracking onshore renminbi interest rates, before rising again in late January, partly owing to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool continued to grow in the second half of 2020. The growth of renminbi deposits accelerated from the fourth quarter, reflecting to some extent the appreciation of the renminbi and higher renminbi interest rates relative to those of other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the growth of the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) accelerated, increasing by 21.9% to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021 (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of the total, renminbi customer deposits increased by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, outstanding CDs decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong As for other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion in the seven-month period since the end of June 2020. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow strongly. From July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, up by 16.7% from the same period a year earlier. Among these transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland increased more than remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong’s deep renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payment and financial transactions. For 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system stayed high at RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Amid the prolonged economic recession caused by recurring waves of the coronavirus pandemic and the prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while their asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient, underpinned by strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures to continue supporting the broader economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, while the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and lingering geopolitical tensions will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impacts of the related downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, from 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed to 1.01% in the second half of 2020 from 1.63% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that outweighed the slight increase in non-interest income and led to lower profits. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 29.4%, while the return on assets fell to 0.77% from 1.19% in 2019. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely due to substantial fund inflows driven by equity market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. HIBORs softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR declined by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, declining notably to 0.28% at the end of 2020 from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates More broadly, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong declined moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks’ net interest margins. In addition, despite breakthroughs in vaccine development that have strengthened market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of the economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the banking sector’s loan quality and profitability in the near term. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio stood at 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated stable funding positions of authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2020, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions hovered at 56.1%, similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans declined during the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell to 72.3% at the end of 2020 from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency deposits. Accordingly, the average Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratios declined to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively at the end of 2020, from 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a prolonged economic recession caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances declined moderately in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, total bank credit still recorded positive growth, although the pace of growth slowed markedly to 1.2% from 6.7% in 2019. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 1.8% in the second half of 2020, after increasing by 3.0% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, after growing by 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans remained broadly unchanged at the end of 2020 compared with the end of June, after declining by 2.0% in the first half. Foreign currency loans declined by 4.5% in the second half of 2020 after surging by 10.6% in the first half, partly reflecting lower demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector became slightly more optimistic about the near-term credit demand outlook compared with six months earlier. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the share of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase in the next three months rose to 37%, while the share expecting loan demand to decline over the same period decreased to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and corporates, banks’ loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose moderately to 0.9% at the end of 2020 from 0.79% six months earlier, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions increased to 0.57% at the end of 2020 from 0.49% at the end of June 2020. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy weakened, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across economies, particularly in the US. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks and the possibility of more aggressive-than-expected monetary policy tightening if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than expected. Should the US Fed tighten monetary policy sharply and thereby tighten global financial conditions, the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies (EMEs) would come under pressure. More recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have significant repercussions for the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, growth in total bank lending accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market softened from mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the ongoing economic recovery, while the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected. These risk factors will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness extending into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to tighter mobility restrictions worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks weighed on production. Meanwhile, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify amid demand-supply imbalances and labour shortages, and have broadened across a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies (AEs), particularly the US. More recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices could further heighten the threat of global inflation, while increased financial market volatility could lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties. In the near term, the reimposition of lockdown measures and renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out in the event of large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks. In the US, as the risk of inflation proving more persistent and broad-based than expected has increased, the US Fed has turned hawkish, accelerating the timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. If the US Fed needs to tighten monetary policy sharply, global financial conditions may also tighten, worsening borrowers’ debt servicing ability, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable EMEs. More recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may pose the risk of sustained increases in global commodity prices, exacerbate shortages of industrial goods and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressure on open-ended funds and increase their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although its momentum temporarily moderated as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed stringent COVID-19 restrictions in the third quarter, while regional exporters of technology products (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from robust global demand for technology products. Although emerging Asia is widely expected to see a broad-based recovery in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for regional economies with lower vaccination rates and constrained public health resources. Second, accelerated policy normalisation by the US Fed could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures. For regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery, the trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, slower growth in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, increases in various commodity prices triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will pass through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Together with increased global economic uncertainty, this will further complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. Over the longer term, to rebuild sustainable and resilient growth models, investors need to attach greater importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is affected by firms’ environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021 amid a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term amid the prolonged property market downturn and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. The Mainland authorities have therefore made stabilising growth their top priority for the year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Total onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both decreased in the second half of 2021. Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remained manageable, as Mainland banks, particularly systemically important banks, had limited exposures to property developer loans, low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP) grew moderately, as merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the continued global economic recovery, improving local labour market conditions and the Government’s rollout of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year expansion since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local COVID-19 infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures weighed on local economic activity. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flows, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and their application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA and the banking sector also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong’s economy is expected to continue to recover in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s implementation of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in the range of 2.0% to 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to the uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly those relating to the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining to 3.9% at year-end. Total employment rebounded, but remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data showed renewed strains in the labour market amid a new wave of local COVID-19 infections. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also indicated fewer new job vacancies. The new wave of local COVID-19 infections and tighter anti-epidemic measures will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in face-to-face contact-intensive sectors. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local COVID-19 situation and the pace of the domestic economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures broadly increased in recent months, but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up in recent months, partly due to increases in the prices of meals out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-induced disruptions to logistics. However, soft rentals and mild domestic labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts headline inflation of 2.4% in 2022, while the Government projects headline and underlying inflation rates of 2.1% and 2.0% respectively. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local equity market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly at one point in October 2021, its strengthening momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen alongside the US Fed’s monetary policy normalisation. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone most of the time and continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Amid ample interbank liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages increased slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to flourish. In particular, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022. Although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased to RMB1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from its efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increasing demand for renminbi assets from international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings, major global equity markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, driving the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in AEs amid sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices and escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict have led major global equity markets to consolidate since early January 2022.

Global economic growth slowed visibly in late 2021 amid the rapid worldwide spread of the Delta and Omicron variants and persistent production bottlenecks, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and broadened across a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies (AEs), particularly the US. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the US Federal Reserve (Fed)’s monetary policy stance, heightening the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions could place the prevailing elevated asset valuations under pressure and weigh on emerging markets, where recoveries generally continued to lag. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant in the region, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with the region’s major exporters of technology products continuing to outperform other economies. While the Omicron variant is unlikely to cause serious disruption to the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cloud the regional economic outlook. In addition, the US Fed’s policy normalisation may trigger corrections in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies may weigh on the region’s merchandise export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, has led to higher commodity prices and increased inflation risks and, on the other hand, will weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, complicating regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021 amid a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power shortages and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressures arising from a cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the Government has made stabilising growth its top priority for the year, and macroeconomic policies will become more supportive. The global economic recovery slowed visibly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant spread on top of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tightened mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply chain problems, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drags from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major AEs, and moderating growth momentum in Mainland China, which offset the expected rebound in growth in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF projections of real GDP growth Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to rise during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) increased visibly in major AEs, particularly the US, where larger-scale policy stimulus had been implemented since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures broadened across a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up the prices of a wide range of commodities, which may exacerbate the already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core consumer price index inflation in selected economies (1) The latest data for the US, the UK and the Euro area are for January 2022, while those for the remaining economies are for December 2021. (2) “Asian advanced economies” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) “Asian emerging market economies” include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties and tilted to the downside, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment unfolds, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less stringent measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, in the event of large-scale outbreaks, the reimposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could lead to renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index – suppliers’ delivery times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments may make the prevailing high global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk of commodity price increases arising from the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia, the lagged pass-through of higher production costs to final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier surge in global residential property prices may drive future rental increases, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the US Fed shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting in December 2021, ceased characterising high inflation as “transitory”, doubled the pace of tapering its asset purchases from US$15 billion to US$30 billion per month with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and began discussing balance sheet reduction. Indeed, recent market pricing suggested that the US Fed might raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. By contrast, given the Euro area’s closer trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face a more significant policy trade-off. Against this backdrop, coupled with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated after a prolonged period of accommodative policies, should persistent inflationary pressures require the US Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt servicing ability could be at risk of deterioration and financial market volatility could be triggered. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe escalated, risk aversion in financial markets increased and signs of US dollar shortages emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Amid premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to a renewed growth slowdown, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds (OEFs), increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for OEFs, can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as the region’s major exporters of technology products, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the uneven recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures remained moderate in many emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index Emerging Asia is widely expected to see a broad-based recovery in 2022, but the near-term regional economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread across the region since late 2021, its economic impact has remained milder than that of previous waves of infection. However, some regional economies where vaccination rates continue to lag and public health resources are more constrained will remain exposed to the threat of new variants. Second, the US Fed’s policy normalisation may trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressures on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support their economic recoveries will face a more difficult trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, the risk of a sudden surge in long-term US yields could also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), intensifying the risk of corrections in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the outlook for regional merchandise trade is subject to uncertainties arising from slowing growth in major economies and a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which could weaken the region’s export growth. Chart 2.6 US: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP Fourth, while regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, commodity price increases triggered by the conflict will pass through to regional inflation and weaken consumption at the same time. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, this will complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted regional economies to the need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models over the longer term in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms’ environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic dealt a severe blow to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some OEFs experienced substantial fund outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Fund outflows from selected OEFs during the March 2020 episode Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another possible reason for the substantial fund outflows was that investors exercised a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming their fund holdings early, thereby avoiding the redemption costs that could surge during periods of market stress. To contain fund outflows arising from the first-mover advantage, some OEFs adopt swing pricing — an OEF pricing rule that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many OEFs used swing pricing during the episode, no empirical research had established whether swing pricing could effectively reduce outflows from OEFs. Against this backdrop, this box conducts an empirical study to examine whether swing pricing reduced fund outflows from OEFs during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. In addition, this box identifies factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we put forward policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors and thereby passing redemption costs on to them. First-mover advantage mainly exists in OEFs that adopt conventional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs incurred by fund investors, such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments, are reflected in OEF prices only after transactions have taken place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear these transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, particularly when substantial redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during periods of market stress, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by OEFs.

Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021 amid sustained growth in merchandise exports and private consumption, recording its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Moving into 2022, a new wave of the local epidemic and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on local economic activities. The overall economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the recovery will be subject to uncertainties and risks relating to the epidemic and US monetary policy normalisation. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up in the near term alongside rising import prices, soft local rentals and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth moderated compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, private consumption increased amid improving labour market conditions and the Government’s implementation of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. However, aggregate investment spending declined in the final quarter following strong rebounds in the preceding two consecutive quarters. Externally, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance remained robust amid the continued global economic recovery, while trade in services remained weak, partly because inbound tourism was still at a standstill (Chart 3.2). On a net basis, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volumes A new wave of the local epidemic and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on local economic activities in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the Special 100% Personal Loan Guarantee and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme would be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and their application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also offered borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which was also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong’s economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the lingering pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from the expansion of the global economy. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in the range of 2.0% to 3.5% in 2022, while the growth forecasts by international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in previous chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the faster pace of US monetary policy normalisation and heightened geopolitical concerns, such as the Russia-Ukraine situation, have clouded the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the rest of the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China may stimulate local economic growth. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining to 3.9% at the end of the year (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, albeit still below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that pressures on the labour market had re-emerged amid a new wave of the local epidemic. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected fewer new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of the local epidemic and the tightening of anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on local epidemic developments and the pace of the domestic economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures generally increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, amid the recovery in domestic demand and rising external prices (Chart 3.5), prices of meals out and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the CCPI continued to decline generally, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Despite remaining soft, real unit labour costs edged up in recent quarters, partly reflecting an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong’s import prices Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.7 Unit labour costs Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-induced disruptions to logistics. However, soft rentals and moderate domestic labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts headline inflation to reach 2.4% in 2022, while the Government forecasts headline and underlying inflation rates of 2.1% and 2.0% respectively for 2022.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period amid risk-off sentiment in the local equity market and concerns over US monetary policy normalisation. With ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) continued to stay low. Overall, the HKD exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is well able to withstand shocks arising from volatilities in fund flows. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone for most of the time, and continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local equity market (Chart 4.1). Despite a mild rebound in October 2021 amid improved market sentiment, the strengthening momentum of the Hong Kong dollar subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak southbound net buying flows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects (Chart 4.2), and market expectations of a stronger US dollar amid an increasingly hawkish outlook for the US Fed’s monetary policy. Initial public offering activities continued to provide support to the Hong Kong dollar during the review period (Chart 4.3). Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there was no sign of unusual cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Net buying through the southbound Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) remained stable due to the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) generally followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds, the pace and magnitude of which will depend on prevailing market conditions, may weaken the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is able to withstand volatilities in fund flows without compromising financial stability. Hong Kong’s monetary environment stayed accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 1.4% in the eight months since end-June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuance to meet banks’ continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, with the Aggregate Balance before Discount Window activities declining correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, Government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) In the six months since end-July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) increased modestly by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. It should, however, be noted that monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering (IPO) related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities. It is therefore more appropriate to observe the longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Overall, Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. With ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBORs continued to stay low despite market concerns over US monetary policy tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of increased funding demand towards the year-end, HIBORs edged up in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer in the event of large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The offshore renminbi (CNH) interbank market continued to function normally during the review period. Amid seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, the overnight CNH HIBOR witnessed mild fluctuations in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) increased by 30.3% in the six months since end-July 2021 to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among the total, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in outstanding CDs. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong During the six-month period since July 2021, although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022 (Chart 4.10), up by 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion during the same period a year earlier. The deep renminbi liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to support a large amount of renminbi payments and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Flows of renminbi trade settlement payments Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Major global equity markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated from January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stances of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. The Hong Kong equity market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by sharp declines in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding pandemic developments in Hong Kong pushed the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi debt market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market softened from mid-2021, partly due to weakened asset market sentiment and a new wave of the local pandemic. Major global equity markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, driving the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). The global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings, underpinned by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, supported the rally in major global equity markets, although the pandemic remained investors’ key risk concern throughout the year. However, major global equity markets consolidated from early January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stances of major central banks in advanced economies in the face of surging inflation risks, sharp increases in commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. By contrast, the Hong Kong equity market continued to lag behind other major global equity markets towards the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index traded between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November and closed at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, renewed buying interest from value investors in the Hong Kong equity market drove the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding pandemic developments in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a near two-year low of 22,713 points at the end of February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index declined by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 The Hang Seng Index and the MSCI World Index Equity market implied volatilities fluctuated sharply in late November 2021 due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, before easing thereafter. Although the SKEW Index retreated from its record high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors’ concerns over a correction in the prolonged equity market rally since the outbreak of the pandemic and hence their willingness to pay more for downside protection (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and the S&P 500 Index, and the SKEW Index Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong equity market continued to register net inflows from international investors since the previous report (Chart 4.13). By contrast, the southbound Stock Connect recorded substantial net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of changes in Mainland regulations on technology stocks. However, buying flows through the southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, registering total inflows of HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, the cumulative net buying amount increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net equity market fund flows into Hong Kong Chart 4.14 Net flows through Stock Connect The Hong Kong primary market slowed in the second half of 2021 after raising a record amount of funds in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, there were 98 IPOs, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), with the total amount raised declining by 17.8% from the preceding year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global IPO market, behind only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Initial public offering market in Hong Kong The outlook for the local equity market remains uncertain. Monetary policy easing in the Mainland and more secondary listings of US-listed Chinese companies in Hong Kong’s primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong equity market. However, the equity market still faces numerous headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding local pandemic developments, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and an escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Retail banks’ profitability in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio increased slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by sound capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, the HKMA extended various support measures to further help the economy weather the difficult period. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, while the risk of a faster-than-expected normalisation of US monetary policy will also pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was mainly attributable to decreases in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets declined to 0.59% from 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Reflecting the persistently low interest rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks also remained low at 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA’s additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) edged up in the final quarter of 2021. Nevertheless, given that liquidity in the banking system remained highly abundant, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR increased slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) increased modestly by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Since June 2019, the composite interest rate has been calculated based on the new local “interest rate risk in the banking book” (IRRBB) framework. As such, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those of previous months. From a broader perspective, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong increased slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost was calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Although the normalisation of US monetary policy may herald an improvement in banks’ profitability, the improvement in the near term may be partly offset by two factors. First, although the Fed has indicated that it would raise interest rates multiple times in 2022, past experience suggests that movements in local interest rates may lag behind those in US interest rates, particularly when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains highly abundant. Therefore, it may take more time for an improvement in banks’ net interest margins to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also create uncertainty over the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks’ asset quality and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.2% at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.5), well above the international minimum requirement of 8%. The Tier 1 capital ratio and the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2% respectively during the period. In addition, the Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated AIs recorded a healthy level of 7.9% at the end of 2021, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3%. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Since 1 January 2013, locally incorporated AIs have been required to comply with the revised Basel III capital adequacy framework. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with the data up to December 2012. The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 151.9% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.6), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 59.1% during the same period, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The latest Net Stable Funding Ratios also reflected stable funding positions of AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.3% in the third quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions also recorded a high level of 150.4%, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75%. The data suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.7 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs. At the end of 2021, customer deposits accounted for 57.6% of all AIs’ total liabilities, similar to the level of 57.2% six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 The liability structure of all AIs 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to the percentage of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. In the second half of 2021, total deposits in the banking sector were broadly unchanged, while total loans and advances declined slightly. By contrast, as the decline in Hong Kong dollar deposits exceeded the decline in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio increased slightly to 86.7% from 84.2% six months earlier.
