Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted substantial efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 separately for the first time this year. I hope this report will provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong’s banking system to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and putting our commitments as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation into practice. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA’s key functions. This report sets out our specific measures and work, with the following key highlights: Banks face climate risks in their day-to-day operations. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to strengthen banks’ climate resilience. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and explored how technology could assist banks in assessing the impacts of physical risks. In view of the increasing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we also shared sound practices with the industry on the proper management of these products to help banks strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives to address climate risks and promote the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy, which will enhance financial market transparency and improve the alignment of green finance policies. Internationally, we actively participate in various international organisations to help formulate policies for addressing climate change and assess its implications for financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable finance. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for global bond markets, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth of 42%, with total issuance increasing to US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest centre in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the People’s Government of Hainan Province, once again demonstrating Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The thriving development of Hong Kong’s green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects covering areas such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two “firsts”. In May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion, which were the world’s largest green retail bond issuance at the time. We also assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural tokenised green bond in February 2023. This was the world’s first tokenised green bond issued by a government, and the issuance marked a milestone in successfully combining our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment requires efforts and collaboration across different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to developing the local green taxonomy mentioned above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training for the industry and enhances Hong Kong’s data resources through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance. The Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas, including mandatory climate-related disclosures and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, particularly by setting a target for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced our risk management practices to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and long-term risk-adjusted returns. In addition, to fully capture the opportunities that may arise from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment by the Exchange Fund and identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the portfolio’s long-term returns. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 43% from its 2017 level. Indeed, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to carbon-intensive assets has consistently remained lower than that of the broader market. Going forward, we will continue progressing towards the net-zero target by further integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into our investment management process, actively exercising ownership rights, maintaining collaboration with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is underpinned by three pillars: the environment, our people and social responsibility. On the environment, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and encouraging a more environmentally friendly market in the wider community. On our people, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive workplace. On social responsibility, we are committed to enhancing financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion and actively giving back to the community. Compared with the levels in 2015, when we began tracking our carbon footprint, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption all recorded double-digit reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the near term, our targets are to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this important global issue, we recognise the need to take concrete action, lead by example, and work alongside like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s near-term plans and priorities for addressing climate change across its key functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will devote our utmost efforts to reaching this goal. We are confident that, through the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the wider community, we will successfully address the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote sustainable development in Hong Kong’s financial sector and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development of green and sustainable finance and related best practices. As the banking regulator, we will seek to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate considerations into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector’s “Greenness Baseline”. The HKMA will also support banks’ efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as by exploring different measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regular regulator-led stress-testing exercise for 2023–2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their capacity to withstand climate risks under an enhanced stress-testing framework covering various stress scenarios, including extreme climate events and adverse economic conditions. To foster the healthy development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct an off-site thematic assessment to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to further develop the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector’s green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green taxonomy framework. On market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in increasing green bond issuance under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the scope of the Programme to cover sustainable bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA is also assisting in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and corporates to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the potential for integrating green finance with technology. We will also continue to collaborate with other agencies through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral issues such as capacity building and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will jointly launch various dedicated programmes in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market insights and targeted professional training for banks, and offering practical guidance to help banks formulate roadmaps for developing green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme and expand its influence in Asia. The Alliance will also strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate knowledge sharing on green finance, and spearhead programmes in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards its net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares about its employees, the wider community and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon emissions reduction and encourage staff to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To implement digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications to further improve operational efficiency, while minimising as far as possible the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been working to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system for a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to the impacts of various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has placed particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas including environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how such risks are addressed under the existing Basel Framework. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related considerations into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress and challenges relating to the implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk considerations into its banking supervisory processes and communicated the plan to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 “Risk-based Supervisory Approach” and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, drawing on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular supervisory stress-testing exercise to enable a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its greenness assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks for addressing risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. In view of the growing prevalence of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified some good practices during the thematic reviews and shared them with the industry through a circular issued in December, enabling banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks’ capabilities to manage climate risks. The HKMA has commenced the development of a common platform for banks to assess the impacts of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions could facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices, leveraging advanced analytics and regulatory technology, complemented by fully automated supervisory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the collection of anti-money laundering supervisory data to reduce the manpower burden on banks and paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and improve the consistency of green finance policies, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to develop a local green classification framework. Commonly known as a green taxonomy, a green classification framework classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore the framework’s features and challenges in depth, and is preparing to put forward proposals and conduct a consultation on the framework’s structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognising the potential risks that climate change may pose to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its existing surveillance work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped further enrich climate scenarios to enable central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On the research front, the HKMA conducted a number of applied research projects in 2022 to explore in depth two major topics, namely greenwashing in corporate green bond markets3 and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of these studies facilitate the formulation of policy and regulatory measures to address the implications of climate risks for financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the implications of climate risks for financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared the research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and its Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under the framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps foster international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, while drawing insights from these discussions to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA stepped up its efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategies1. The Steering Group’s work is primarily guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out six key long-term focus areas and five near-term action points to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem for a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre Promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection Enhance the relevant skills of practitioners and raise public awareness and understanding Encourage product innovation and initiatives to channel capital towards green and sustainable projects Capitalise on opportunities presented by the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into the green finance centre of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) Enhance regional and international collaboration Actions taken to date to advance sustainable finance development in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Its current priorities include capacity building and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), green taxonomy (see “Establishing a green classification framework to facilitate green finance” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group announced in March the preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong, and will support Hong Kong’s development into a regional carbon trading centre, including developing a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalising on opportunities arising from GBA collaboration. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability and sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of the collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire for non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which not only facilitates sustainability reporting by companies but also helps financial institutions collect and analyse company-level data for risk assessment and relevant business decisions. This marks an important step in expanding the scope of the Steering Group’s data work to include SMEs, an important segment of the economy that had previously been more difficult to reach. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the efforts of financial regulators, government bureaux and departments, industry stakeholders and academia in capacity building and policy development, and to develop resources and data repositories. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories covering data, training information and internship opportunities respectively to facilitate access by the financial sector and other sectors to green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. The repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong To support capacity building for industry practitioners, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme in December to provide subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and capacity building. Other capacity-building initiatives included launching the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new Green and Sustainable Finance module3 under the HKMA’s Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners. Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the HKMA launched the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks4, a collaborative platform bringing together financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to develop green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to empower commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential in making green finance a mainstream core business and to facilitate the financial system’s participation in global climate-related activities. How it works Provide financial institutions with a one-stop peer-learning platform to access the knowledge, tools and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions Bring together green finance leaders and connect green financial institutions across emerging markets Facilitate dialogue and explore frontier topics Advance the global green finance agenda and unlock unlimited green and climate-related investment opportunities In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became Cornerstone Members of the Alliance and worked closely with the IFC and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices in green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to support the transition to a green economy. In addition, three Global Partners and one Knowledge Partner6 pledged in 2022 to contribute climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone Members, IFC and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has held a total of 18 training events and roundtables, attracting more than 6,000 participants from across the globe, including Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022, the Alliance and the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7 published their first frontier topic research report, entitled “Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulatory Oversight”. The HKMA continued to promote the issuance of green and sustainable debt and foster a local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022, including bonds and loans, reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion) To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of the related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued close to US$16 billion equivalent of institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects covering areas such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the Programme’s transparency and accountability arrangements, the Government publishes a Green Bond Report annually, setting out details of the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable members of the public to participate in and share the benefits of Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment, the inaugural retail green bonds totalling HK$20 billion were issued in May and received an enthusiastic response from the public, making them the world’s largest retail green bond issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong and consolidated Hong Kong’s position as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular institutional green bond issuances in the 2022–23 financial year and issued US$5.75 billion equivalent of green bonds in January 2023. The triple-currency offering, denominated in US dollars, euros and renminbi, comprised tenors ranging from two to 30 years and continued to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The offering was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government’s previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors’ confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The shares taken up by international investors and Mainland investors participating through Southbound Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong’s status as a premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology in bond issuance and settlement. It was the first tokenised green bond issued by a government globally. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis through a private blockchain network, while subsequent processes, including coupon payments, secondary-market trade settlement and redemption at maturity, were also digitalised. The experience gained from this Government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in undertaking similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. According to the International Capital Market Association’s report, Hong Kong became Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances in 2022, with bonds arranged in Hong Kong totalling US$27.8 billion, accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances US$27.8 billion Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB5 billion of offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the People’s Government of Hainan Province also issued its first RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong, including blue and sustainability bonds. These bond issuances once again highlighted Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its longstanding position as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in 2021 and leveraged the Scheme to attract more related professional service providers, including financial institutions, green consultants and external reviewers, to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The Scheme was well received by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the expenses of pre-issuance, post-issuance or both types of external review services for issuers of more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan size threshold for external review cost subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof of concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA collaborated again with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards, also known as mitigation outcome interests (MOIs), with a view to enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022 and successfully developed two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in support of the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission and integrating environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth next”, the HKMA believes that taking environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into account can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate associated risks. In the face of mounting climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a “Net-zero Emissions by 2050” target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategies to strengthen portfolio resilience, thereby achieving better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively contributes to building the green and sustainable finance ecosystem by partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment and collaborating with international organisations to formulate ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Financial Stability Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is that the HKMA will give priority to ESG investments if their risk-adjusted long-term returns are comparable to other investments, in line with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Sub-Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, oversees ESG and climate-related risks arising from the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Sub-Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors progress in ESG integration and the Exchange Fund’s ESG profile through regular meeting reports submitted by the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s various ESG initiatives. The proposals discussed and work progress at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Oversight and governance structure for responsible investment The dedicated team of the Risk Management and Compliance Division works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investments: Public market investments The Credit, Rules and Compliance Committee, comprising the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Compliance Division participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Active Ownership” under the “Risk Management” section on page 27 for details). Private market investments The Investment Sub-Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal conducted by the Risk Management and Compliance Division and the private market investment teams. Concrete evidence² continues to point to the significant impacts of climate change and associated risks. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming that the announced Nationally Determined Contribution targets across jurisdictions are fully implemented, the estimated rise in global temperature by 2100 would still be as high as 2.1°C to 2.4°C, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting the increase in the global average temperature to below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. If jurisdictions adopt more aggressive policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and market repricing of assets in anticipation of future trends, together with inherent physical risks, would intensify pressure on asset valuations. In view of updates to global warming trajectories and modelling assumptions, the HKMA drew on the expertise of external consultants to further assess the resilience of the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” under a “Rapid Transition” scenario (Figure 2), in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021. The “Rapid Transition” scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly lead to a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are abruptly divested to keep the increase in average temperature within 1.5°C by 2100. The scenario is broadly aligned with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The “Investment Portfolio” remains resilient over the medium to long term because a relatively large proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sectoral distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets may benefit from the transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may weigh on performance in the short term, particularly that of equity assets. The “Investment Portfolio” as a whole will be increasingly affected by physical risks that gradually materialise over time. Energy and conventional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Climate scenarios, like other modelling approaches, have their limitations. The analysis is based on the sectoral distribution of market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level and does not take into account the effects of actively selecting specific securities within a sector. More in-depth analysis shows that investments in the “Investment Portfolio” are generally more resilient to, or less affected by, transition shocks than the strategic asset allocation market benchmarks. This result reaffirms that the HKMA’s climate-focused responsible investment approach can enhance portfolio resilience. The climate change trajectory remains uncertain, while scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully recognises the risks and opportunities arising from climate change. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and capturing opportunities relating to climate transition, climate risk mitigation and enhancement of long-term portfolio returns. Building on its strong momentum, the HKMA further increased its holdings of green, social and sustainability bonds by 50% in 2022. For equity investments, the HKMA invests in an actively managed governance-themed equity portfolio and adopts a decarbonisation strategy for passive equity portfolios that tilts towards companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with general partners of the Exchange Fund’s “Long-Term Growth Portfolio” the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Figure 3). Figure 3 Ongoing initiatives to increase ESG investments The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator that, in addition to generating clean energy, places great emphasis on social factors and natural biodiversity. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain species of vultures. Livestock are important assets for local villagers. To help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the animals from natural predators. In addition, the operator employs a bird-monitoring team to issue warnings when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left behind by predators, so that the wind turbines can be shut down to prevent vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win outcome: it safeguards the villagers’ livelihoods while reducing fatal collisions between vultures and wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can create more business opportunities and open up revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply-chain-related operation. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China specialising in cold-chain logistics services for pharmaceuticals, chemical products and high-end consumer goods. The company faces increasingly stringent ESG operating standards, mainly because its multinational corporate clients require service providers to meet ambitious decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these requirements, the company engaged an external consultant to help formulate a “Three-year ESG Plan” to reduce its carbon intensity by 50% by 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan delivered significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG initiatives earned the company the “Low-carbon and Green Management Case” award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and recognition enabled the company to secure considerable business opportunities, particularly from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical products sectors that attach great importance to ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its fourth annual ESG Workshop, exchanging sound ESG practices with nine participating private market institutions, including general partners, limited partners and corporates, and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public market, the HKMA encourages trading counterparties, mainly investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr Howard Lee, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivers opening remarks at the HKMA ESG Workshop 2022 At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in efforts to formulate industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a PRI-coordinated collaborative initiative among signatories to develop standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaires⁵, ⁶ for private equity and venture capital investments, assisting private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in various working groups supporting FCLTGlobal’s research into leading market practices for long-term portfolios and the decarbonisation of private assets, as well as the application of such practices by long-term investors. As an NGFS member and TCFD supporter, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS Guide on Climate-related Disclosure for Central Banks, demonstrating its commitment to adopting sound ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a workstream under the NGFS “Net Zero for Central Banks” workstream and participates in the development of sustainable and responsible investment approaches for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars to share insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. In addition to encouraging staff to undertake sustainability-related courses and obtain relevant qualifications, the HKMA gained relevant knowledge and practical experience through the process of engaging external consultants in 2021 to advise on leading industry practices for portfolio climate transition.
