The HKMA is committed to reducing its institutional carbon footprint, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier and contributing to Hong Kong’s overall climate goals. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also fulfils its commitments to caring for the well-being of its staff, promoting financial inclusion and discharging its social responsibilities. The HKMA is committed to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA puts the principles of sustainability into practice under three pillars: the environment, its people and social responsibility (Diagram 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee is responsible for leading the formulation and implementation of the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives and representatives from the Risk and Compliance Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department, and submits regular reports to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the Committee’s leadership, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing initiatives in their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved climate targets for corporate operations and reviewed the transition roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to review the progress of the HKMA’s green initiatives, including proposals to enhance the HKMA’s sustainable procurement policies, procedures and practices. Sustainability governance structure The HKMA’s corporate sustainability journey In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, its staff and the wider community, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the “15 Years Plus Caring Organisation” logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to its institutional carbon footprint and has formulated internal Green Office Guidelines to manage the environmental impact of its operational processes. The HKMA has incorporated environmental considerations into the interior design, operation, repair and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, the HKMA was awarded a Gold rating under BEAM Plus for certain renovated office areas. This was its second green building certification, following the LEED Gold certification obtained in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interiors Version 1.0 Gold rating The HKMA implemented various energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption⁶ in 2022 was 4,996.4 megawatt-hours (2.8 megawatt-hours per capita⁷), down 24.4% from 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions⁸ in 2022 amounted to 2,996.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per capita), down 38.2% from 2015 (Figure 2). Figure 1 Figure 2 Greenhouse gas emissions intensity (Scopes 1 and 2) The HKMA encourages paperless internal operations. It has also implemented a print management system under which staff are required to log in to printers to confirm each print request, helping reduce unnecessary printing and toner use. Where printing is necessary, double-sided and black-and-white printing are encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic record-keeping system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per capita), down 65.3% from 2015 (Figure A). Figure A: Paper consumption intensity The HKMA’s waste management efforts continued to follow the “4R” principle. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA also reduced electronic waste by adopting technological solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit analysing the composition of waste generated by its offices. The audit found that food waste accounted for a significant proportion of total waste, prompting the HKMA to launch a food waste recycling programme (see “Enhancing Waste Management” on page 41). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022, including general and recyclable waste, amounted to 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per capita), down 4.8% from 2015 (Figure 3). The fluctuations in the trend mainly reflected the work-from-home arrangements implemented at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations following the fifth wave of the pandemic. Figure 3 Non-hazardous waste intensity The HKMA gives priority to waste reduction at source and strives to reduce, reuse and recycle. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste generated in its daily operations, including plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood and electronic products, and to provide recommendations on waste reduction. Based on the audit findings, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, placing food waste collection bins in all pantries. Food waste collected each day is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong and converted into renewable energy for electricity generation. Residues generated during the conversion process can also be turned into compost for landscaping and agricultural production. Recycling bins are also conveniently placed at different locations throughout the offices. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and pays greater attention to further improving source separation of recyclables and the proper handling of recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers and beverage bottles. We also continue to organise activities to raise staff’s environmental awareness, explain waste management policies and encourage staff to make good use of the recycling facilities in the offices. Food waste collected each day is transported to an organic resources recovery centre Recycling plastic items The HKMA operates two data centres, one for operations and the other as a backup. As they account for a major proportion of the organisation’s overall energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green designs and various energy-saving measures, including in-row air-conditioning systems, light-emitting diode lighting and round-the-clock monitoring of power efficiency. Following the completion of a consultancy study on the green performance of these data centres in 2022, the HKMA is preparing to implement recommendations to enhance overall energy efficiency. Preparations have also begun for obtaining green data centre certification. Recognising the importance of fostering a sustainability culture, the HKMA regularly launches various programmes and activities to educate and encourage staff to develop sustainable habits and adopt green and digital ways of working. The HKMA shares green living tips and annual office-wide statistics on energy and paper consumption with staff, reminding them of how they can help address environmental issues at the individual level. Staff are also encouraged to offer suggestions on sustainability matters. Led by a Senior Manager of the Administration Division, a focus group brings together staff from different departments to brainstorm ideas and concrete measures for promoting a green working environment. Focus group members also serve as ambassadors when new green initiatives are introduced. The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt more environmentally friendly practices and has introduced various measures to enhance the operational efficiency of the HKMA, the financial industry and the broader economy while minimising resource consumption. The HKMA’s Submission Through Electronic Transmission system (STET) is a one-stop platform that enables banks to submit documents electronically to the HKMA, covering various regular returns required on a weekly, monthly, quarterly or annual basis. Another system, e-Delivery, is a secure electronic communication channel through which the HKMA issues information such as circulars and guidelines to banks. Both systems help save a substantial amount of paper each year. In handling banking complaints and enforcement work, the HKMA has adopted measures to support paperless document submission, enabling bank customers to lodge complaints through electronic channels and online forms. The HKMA is also developing a next-generation management information system to facilitate complaint handling and the transition from paper to digital records. To reduce paper consumption, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU)⁹ has adopted digital signatures in its daily communications with participants, including the issuance of circulars, account-opening and account-termination letters, and responses to audit confirmations. Looking ahead, the CMU will continue to explore further green initiatives, including the adoption of automated electronic processes for internal and external communications. The HKMA encourages the public to make greater use of electronic payments instead of cash and physical cheques by promoting the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored value facilities. More information on FPS and stored value facilities is provided in the chapter “Hong Kong as an International Financial Centre” of the HKMA Annual Report 2022. Distributing electronic lai see is simple and convenient, and reduces the use of physical lai see envelopes and banknotes, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s sustainable development. To this end, the HKMA continued to promote electronic lai see actively through various social and traditional media platforms, encouraging the public to distribute electronic lai see via FPS or other e-wallet services using online or mobile banking services during the Lunar New Year. Major banks and e-wallet operators also organised various activities to attract users to electronic lai see, such as offering festive user interfaces, enhancing functionality for greater convenience, and launching lucky draws or cash rebates. The HKMA promotes electronic lai see on social media For members of the public who choose to distribute physical lai see during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA continues to encourage the use of “good-as-new notes”, namely used notes that remain in good condition, for filling lai see envelopes. Good-as-new notes reduce the need to print new banknotes, thereby reducing the environmental impact. Feedback from note-issuing banks indicates that public acceptance of good-as-new notes has increased in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts to promote coin recycling. Coins collected under the Programme are recirculated to meet public demand, improving the efficiency of coin circulation and reducing the need for minting. The Programme operates two Coin Carts and has so far served more than one million customers, collecting over 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HK$1.3 billion. In 2022, around 78% of users chose to use some or all of the value of their coins to top up their stored value facility accounts. The HKMA has maintained its collaboration with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service by deploying Coin Carts to collect coins on flag days organised by non-governmental organisations, thereby supporting social services. Coin-counting machine on a Coin Cart Launched in 2014, the Coin Collection Programme is the world’s first systematic coin collection programme using a mobile vehicle concept. Over the years, it has received numerous local and international awards in recognition of its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin handling. The Programme operates two Coin Carts, each equipped with two high-speed coin-counting machines to collect coins exchanged by members of the public. Members of the public may choose to exchange their coins for banknotes, top up stored value facility accounts such as Octopus cards or e-wallets, or donate the proceeds to the Community Chest. In addition to collecting coins, the Coin Carts are occasionally deployed for various educational activities, such as student visits.

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency conducted an independent verification of the climate targets (“Climate Targets”) of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (“HKMA”). The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual (“SBTi Corporate Manual”). The objective of this verification was to verify whether the Climate Targets were developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. The verification was conducted in accordance with International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information”, issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to form an opinion and conclusion to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in accordance with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the information. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. Shum Siu Yan Head of Audit Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency March 2023 Verification Statement Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency conducted an independent verification of the 2022 environmental data (“2022 Data”) of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (“HKMA”). The 2022 Data include total energy consumption, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions intensity, paper consumption intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rate for 2022, as well as changes in these data compared with 2015 levels. The HKMA’s greenhouse gas emissions data were compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (“GHG Protocol”) jointly published by the World Resources Institute (“WRI”) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (“WBCSD”). The scope of verification covered the relevant data for the period from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2022, as well as the relevant data for the period from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015 used for year-on-year performance comparison. The scope of verification covered a total of six office and warehouse premises, comprising four offices at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place and 4) Kowloon Commerce Centre, and two warehouses at 5) Rockson Industrial Centre and 6) Tsuen Lee Centre, located in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The objective of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance as to the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA’s data collection mechanism. Within the scope of verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency reviewed selected representative data and supporting evidence from the six premises. The verification was conducted in accordance with International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information”, issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to form an opinion and conclusion to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in accordance with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The completeness and accuracy of the data were tested by tracing selected sample data back to their sources. The underlying procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation and internal checking were also reviewed and tested for reliability. The verification process also included verifying the internal data collection and management mechanism, interviewing representatives responsible for preparing the 2022 Data, and selecting representative data and information for examination. The relevant source data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the information. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. The verification team of Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency was not involved in the preparation of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance over the 2022 Data and concludes that: • The 2022 Data are materially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA’s overall data collection mechanism is adequate. Shum Siu Yan Head of Audit Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency March 2023

Scaling up and accelerating climate action has become one of the most pressing issues of our time. Nearly half of this critical decade for the climate has already passed. We need to reduce global carbon emissions by more than 40% within this decade to have any hope of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Yet greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach record highs. The latest climate science indicates that the window of opportunity to limit the global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius will soon close. The impacts of a 1.1-degree Celsius rise in temperature are already evident to all—extreme weather events such as record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding and storms are occurring with increasing frequency and intensity around the world. Hong Kong is no exception. Last September, immediately after being battered by a powerful super typhoon, we experienced a once-in-a-century rainstorm. Despite our sound infrastructure and swift disaster response capabilities, the impacts were still severe—widespread flooding, transport disruptions and damage to roads in many areas. All these serve as a clear reminder that decisive and ambitious climate action cannot wait. Asia faces particularly significant challenges in its low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development and sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that strike an appropriate balance between climate action, economic growth and social inclusion. This is by no means easy. Given the region’s rapid economic development and population growth, it accounts for more than half of global carbon emissions. At the same time, the Asia-Pacific region is also vulnerable to rising sea levels and extreme weather because of its high population density and geographical location. As economies in the region are at different stages of development, the low-carbon transition will create new opportunities for some, but raising the necessary transition finance will pose an enormous challenge for others. Market estimates suggest that the Asia-Pacific region will require more than US$3 trillion in low-carbon transition investment annually over the next 30 years. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong has both the capability and the responsibility to harness the power of finance to support the low-carbon transition across Asia. As a banking regulator, market facilitator and responsible investor, the HKMA has been devoting significant efforts to the sustainability agenda. The various concrete measures and initiatives undertaken by the HKMA over the past year are set out in the different chapters of this report. In addition, to strengthen the HKMA’s internal governance structure and more effectively coordinate sustainability efforts across different functional areas, we established the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee last year. Details of the Steering Committee can be found in the new chapter on “Sustainability Governance”. Hong Kong banks play an important role in supporting Asia’s transition to net zero. In addition to performing our traditional role as a banking regulator by ensuring in our day-to-day supervision that banks properly manage climate risks, we also act as a facilitator to support the banking sector in financing the low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green classification framework to help banks and other financial institutions identify environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate goals. We launched a prototype green classification framework for consultation in May and are now refining it in light of the feedback received during the consultation. In addition, amid the growing need for higher-quality and more globally comparable sustainability disclosures, the HKMA is working with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board in June, which provide a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator is not limited to developing frameworks and rules; we are also committed to addressing the pain points faced by the industry. At present, many banks find it difficult to conduct physical risk assessments because of data constraints. In view of this, the HKMA will shortly launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform. By simply entering a property address, banks will be able to assess the impacts of physical hazards on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios, thereby helping them manage the associated climate risks. As a major international financial centre and sustainable finance hub in Asia, Hong Kong has long served as a bridge channelling international investment into sustainable development projects in Asia and supporting the region’s low-carbon transition. In recent years, international green and sustainable bonds arranged in Hong Kong have accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, significantly ahead of other jurisdictions. Particularly noteworthy is that the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong in 2023 for the third and second consecutive years respectively, once again affirming Hong Kong’s important role as a green gateway connecting the Mainland with the rest of the world. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s sustainable bond market is attributable in part to the demonstration effect of the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing approximately US$25 billion worth of green bonds to institutional and retail investors. With each issuance, we have seized the opportunity to innovate and broaden the features of green bonds, including their currencies, tenors and distribution channels, laying the groundwork for other public- and private-sector green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bond in 2022, we issued the world’s first tokenised government green bond in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the second tokenised green bond issuance. Denominated in four major currencies and issued in digitally native form, these were the world’s first multi-currency digital green bonds. At the same time, we have proactively introduced various measures to enhance the vibrancy and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem. These encompass work in areas such as capacity building, data enhancement, green fintech and transition finance. In talent development in particular, we launched a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners in 2023, providing banking practitioners with a structured curriculum to deepen their understanding and professional knowledge of green and sustainable finance. Transition finance is another key area of our work. It provides funding for decarbonisation activities in high-emitting and hard-to-abate sectors, preventing these sectors from failing to transition because of a lack of financial support. To support the sound development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand Hong Kong’s green classification framework to cover transition activities. We will also broaden the scope of the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme, which provides subsidies to eligible bond issuers and borrowers, to include transition bonds and loans, thereby encouraging corporates in the region to raise transition finance in Hong Kong. In addition, we will strengthen engagement with relevant stakeholders and attract private-sector investment into sustainable development projects that have traditionally found it more difficult to secure financing through public-private partnerships and blended finance. Some of the above initiatives require cross-sectoral collaboration and are coordinated mainly by the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional collaboration is equally important. In addition to our longstanding collaboration with the International Finance Corporation on the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office also became a founding member of the Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership in 2023. The Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero also announced plans to establish a chapter in Hong Kong. Through these partnerships, we hope to promote capacity building and knowledge sharing, thereby supporting the channelling of capital into sustainable development projects across the region and around the world. To promote new business development and knowledge exchange, the HKMA also helped organise the inaugural Hong Kong Green Week earlier this year, attracting more than 1,600 participants from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including leading decision-makers from the global business and financial communities, to discuss ways to scale up climate finance in the region and forge new partnerships in this area. Chief Executive Eddie Yue delivers remarks at the Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum, the flagship event of Hong Kong Green Week. As the manager of Hong Kong’s official reserves and a major global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of investing in green and sustainable assets and has progressively expanded the Exchange Fund’s portfolio of ESG and green assets in the public and private markets. In support of the goal of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s Investment Portfolio by 2050 or earlier, the HKMA added an actively managed global equity portfolio with a sustainability and climate transition theme last year, while extending the application of a customised low-carbon equity index to another public-market asset portfolio. In addition, the green, social and sustainability bonds prioritised by the HKMA have outperformed their investment benchmarks, demonstrating the proposition of “doing well by doing good”. In the private markets, we continued to pursue green-related investment opportunities and became an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. At the end of 2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had declined by 6% and 46% from its 2021 and 2017 levels respectively, and remained below the overall market level. As a sustainable organisation, the HKMA will continue to strive for improvement and formulate our sustainability goals and plans around the three pillars of environment, people and social responsibility. Specifically, along our low-carbon transition journey, the HKMA continues to strengthen its capacity to address climate change by assessing our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures cover emissions reduction, energy efficiency enhancement and waste management, with the ultimate objective of fulfilling our commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We have formulated plans to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely in the near term and are making good progress towards our interim target for reducing Scope 2 emissions by 2030. Beyond green objectives, the HKMA is also committed to promoting the physical and mental well-being of its staff in order to attract and retain outstanding talent to discharge its important functions. In addition, by collaborating with various stakeholders to promote financial inclusion, enhance the public’s financial literacy and raise public awareness of financial fraud, we contribute to building a caring society. The climate challenge is immense and exceptionally urgent. As economies around the world move towards a more sustainable future, the process is expected to bring about enormous changes in financing activities and asset allocation. This transformation entails considerable risks, but will also be accompanied by unprecedented opportunities. As a leading global sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has a responsibility to take the lead in addressing these challenges. At the same time, we are well positioned to build on this momentum. The HKMA will fully support the industry in financing the low-carbon transition; continue to lead by example as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation; and work with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

Climate change risks and other sustainability issues are global in nature. The HKMA’s sustainability objective is to lead by example through its policies and operations, ensuring that both Hong Kong’s financial system and the HKMA itself are resilient to climate change risks, while supporting the transition to a more sustainable economy. Through active participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also seek to contribute to the formulation of green and sustainable finance policies and standards at both regional and global levels. As the banking regulator, the HKMA will further strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. Specifically, key priorities include: conducting a new round of thematic examinations of banks’ climate risk management practices and a new round of consultation sessions as part of the review of banks’ progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management; continuing the work of incorporating climate considerations into the HKMA’s supervisory review process; completing the second round of the sector-wide climate risk stress test, providing guidance to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing observations and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures, including working with relevant local authorities to align the related requirements with the International Financial Reporting Standards Sustainability Disclosure Standards as the global baseline, and preparing for implementation of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s Pillar 3 framework1 for climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidance on best practices in transition planning with the industry. To foster the healthy development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will continue to keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments and maintain engagement with the industry to ensure that banks adopt appropriate sales processes. In addition, the HKMA will act as a facilitator to foster the development of the green finance ecosystem and support banks in financing the economic transition. We will shortly publish the local green taxonomy and continue to expand its coverage to encompass more activities, including transition activities. Meanwhile, we will continue to explore the application of technology solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures; one example is the forthcoming cloud-based platform to facilitate banks’ physical risk assessments. To enhance practitioners’ professional capabilities, we will also develop the professional level of the Green and Sustainable Finance module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners in 2024. Hong Kong is well positioned to serve as a regional and international sustainable finance hub. To fulfil this role, the HKMA is assisting the Government in implementing the proposal in the 2023–24 Budget to expand the scope of the Government Green Bond Programme to cover sustainable finance projects, thereby deepening the development of the local green and sustainable bond market, while attracting more green financing activities, including transition finance activities, to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. We will also continue to encourage more governments, institutions and corporates to raise green funds through Hong Kong and explore potential synergies between green finance and technology. In addition, we will continue to assist in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. As Co-Chair of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), we will continue to work closely with other agencies and departments to co-ordinate cross-sectoral policies and initiatives for promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In 2024, the Steering Group will focus on three areas, namely sustainability disclosures, the application of technology and transition finance. As another priority, through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will continue to jointly launch various dedicated programmes in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing insightful market analysis, delivering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help financial institutions develop their distinctive green transition pathways. In 2024, we will also seek to deepen collaboration with the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, the Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership. As a responsible investor, the HKMA is committed to achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s Investment Portfolio by 2050 or earlier. We will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments through a three-pronged responsible investment approach, ensuring the resilience of the portfolio throughout the journey towards net zero. Recognising that the goals of the Paris Agreement can only be achieved through an economy-wide transition, we are refining our net-zero strategy to focus on assets that can deliver positive climate benefits to the real economy, while taking into account the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. As an environmentally responsible organisation, the HKMA’s decarbonisation strategy will continue to evolve in response to the latest market, regulatory, technological and other climate-related developments. To further strengthen the HKMA’s climate resilience and risk preparedness, we will explore the feasibility of using technology solutions to assess the impact of physical risks on our offices. In addition, we will continue to actively encourage staff participation in our sustainability efforts, including launching campaigns to promote sustainable habits and enhancing office processes and practices. The HKMA will also continue to maintain a consistent, efficient and sustainable procurement approach, including assessing suppliers’ ESG practices when selecting suppliers and renewing contracts. Building on the green data centre certification obtained in 2023, the HKMA is committed to upholding the specified certification standards. When periodically upgrading our data centre facilities, we will not only keep abreast of the latest technological developments but also incorporate green designs and practices. Meanwhile, we will continue to reduce electronic waste through the application and consolidation of technology, and actively modernise our internal systems to enhance efficiency and minimise potential risks as far as possible. Finally, in respect of our social focus, the HKMA will identify more community service opportunities for colleagues and work with the industry to promote financial inclusion and financial literacy, as well as raise public awareness of financial fraud prevention.

Climate change affects every aspect of human life, and everyone can contribute to mitigating its impacts. Through its multiple roles as a central banking institution, banking regulator, market facilitator, responsible investor and sustainable organisation, the HKMA contributes to promoting and accelerating the transition to net-zero emissions in Hong Kong and across Asia. The HKMA has established a robust sustainability governance framework to guide the formulation of its related strategies and policies, oversee the implementation of related initiatives, and ensure that sustainability considerations are incorporated into its own operations and practices. In its commitment to good corporate governance, the HKMA has established a robust sustainability governance framework for its sustainability-related work, with clear accountability arrangements and a high degree of transparency. The governance framework ensures that sustainability considerations are effectively integrated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, with effective mechanisms in place to monitor and evaluate the progress and effectiveness of its sustainability work. The HKMA’s sustainability governance framework comprises: the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant sub-committees, which oversee and advise on the HKMA’s work, including its sustainability work; the Green and Sustainability Steering Committee (Steering Committee), chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, which leads the HKMA’s overall environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategies and policies at the management level; for responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, which coordinates and oversees ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office; and, for other functional areas, relevant teams and working groups, which plan and implement related sustainability initiatives covering banking and market development as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (CASG), co-initiated by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the efforts of financial regulators, government bureaux and departments, industry stakeholders and other stakeholders to accelerate the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. Given the significant expansion in the scope of the HKMA’s sustainability work over the past few years, we established the Steering Committee in October as a new central platform to lead and more effectively coordinate all sustainability work across the HKMA’s different functional areas1. It provides guidance on the formulation of strategies, policies and plans for ESG-related matters across the four functional areas of banking, market development, Exchange Fund investment and internal operations; oversees the implementation of ESG-related plans by the HKMA’s various functional departments; evaluates the HKMA’s performance and effectiveness in achieving its ESG objectives; and oversees external communication strategies. The Steering Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with the three Deputy Chief Executives serving as standing members. The Executive Directors responsible for key functions related to green and sustainability matters are also invited to attend Steering Committee meetings to report on the key outcomes of their work and future plans. The Steering Committee meets regularly and is supported by relevant working groups under the HKMA’s banking departments, Corporate Development and Services Division, External Department and Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition to formulating and implementing its own sustainability initiatives, the HKMA and the SFC co-initiated the CASG in May 20202. As a cross-agency platform, the CASG provides strategic direction and coordinates cross-sectoral efforts by the financial sector to address climate and environmental risks, with a view to consolidating Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance centre in Asia and globally. For details of the CASG’s work, see the chapter “Strengthening the Green and Sustainable Finance Ecosystem”.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been working to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system for a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainability agenda. Banks are affected by various sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has focused particularly on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA is committed to developing various policy measures to enhance the banking system’s resilience to climate risks. In August, the HKMA issued a circular on net-zero transition planning, setting out high-level principles to assist banks in maintaining safety and soundness during the transition to a net-zero economy. Following the issuance of the circular, we conducted a questionnaire survey of selected banks in the fourth quarter to understand their transition planning practices. Based on the survey results, we will share observations and sound practices on transition planning with the industry, and organise seminars or workshops to facilitate the exchange of experience within the industry. Regarding disclosure requirements, in light of the latest international developments, including the publication of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards in June and the consultation launched by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee) in November on a Pillar 3 disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks, the HKMA is stepping up its efforts to refine the sustainability-related disclosure framework for banks in Hong Kong. Specifically, the HKMA is working with relevant local authorities and stakeholders to develop a comprehensive roadmap for Hong Kong that is aligned with the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. During the year, the HKMA strengthened its supervision of banks’ climate risk management and provided recommendations to help banks further enhance their climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA made significant progress in implementing its two-year plan to incorporate climate risk considerations into its banking supervisory processes. Climate risk management has now become a standing agenda item at prudential meetings with bank management. Banking supervisors also apply the enhanced CAMEL rating system1, which has incorporated climate risk considerations, to assess banks’ risk profiles and risk management systems. As part of implementing the two-year plan to incorporate climate risk considerations into its banking supervisory processes, the HKMA revised its “greenness” assessment framework to focus on banks’ transition planning practices. The HKMA is also reviewing its supervisory review process for assessing and monitoring banks’ capital adequacy and determining their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks for climate risks. Following the end of the 12-month implementation period for compliance with Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management”, a key work priority under the two-year plan in 2023, the HKMA commenced a round of thematic reviews on climate-related risk governance in the second quarter. The thematic review covered four major areas, namely the governance framework for climate-related risks, oversight of climate strategy, oversight of climate-related risk management, and organisational culture, awareness and communication. The HKMA made various enhancements to the climate risk stress testing framework, including the introduction of a new five-year scenario to assess the potential impact on banks of simultaneous economic and climate change shocks. Following these enhancements and as part of the HKMA’s regular supervisor-led stress testing programme, the second round of climate risk stress testing was launched in June to conduct a comprehensive assessment of banks’ climate risk exposures and further enhance banks’ capabilities to manage climate risks. A total of 44 banks participated in this climate risk stress test, representing an increase of more than 60% compared with the inaugural pilot exercise in 2021. The HKMA also organised a Climate Risk Stress Testing Forum in November, which was attended by as many as 300 banking practitioners. By facilitating the sharing of experience among banks, the event helped deepen the industry’s overall understanding of climate risk measurement. The HKMA also conducted a series of consultation meetings to review banks’ progress in implementing Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management”. The HKMA held meetings with bank management to discuss their climate risk management efforts and the common challenges facing the industry, and reviewed information provided by banks and other publicly available information to assess their progress. The HKMA provided banks with targeted recommendations to encourage and support them in continuing to strengthen their climate risk management capabilities in line with the HKMA’s supervisory expectations. As global attention to and efforts to address climate change continue to grow, the HKMA has observed increasing demand for green and sustainable investment products, with some banks offering related products to meet customer demand. In view of this, the HKMA completed a thematic review of banks’ sale of green and sustainable investment products and issued a circular in November setting out the standards that banks are expected to meet and sharing observed sound practices. The circular covers various areas, including product due diligence, disclosure, governance and controls, staff training and bookbuilding, and aims to mitigate potential greenwashing risks and enhance investor confidence, thereby promoting the sound development of related investment activities. The HKMA will continue to monitor the latest trends and market developments. The HKMA is committed to promoting the use of technology in green and sustainable banking. For example, technology can enhance data availability and risk analytics, thereby strengthening banks’ capabilities to manage climate risks. The HKMA will shortly launch a pilot cloud-based platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on residential and commercial buildings under different climate scenarios. In addition, the HKMA continues to collaborate with other central banks and regulators to explore how technological solutions can facilitate physical risk assessments. Meanwhile, the HKMA also encourages the adoption of sustainable anti-money laundering (AML) practices through advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to reduce the consumption of compliance-related resources. In 2023, the HKMA launched an online shared data submission platform to fully automate the financial crime risk data collection process, thereby enhancing banks’ operational processes for the sustainable submission of AML-related data. In September, the HKMA organised the Green Fintech Competition to identify market-ready solutions that could help the banking industry address challenges in the following areas: (i) net-zero transition or transition planning; (ii) climate risk management; (iii) green and sustainable finance; and (iv) sustainability- or climate-related disclosure and reporting. The competition attracted more than 85 entries from around 70 companies. In December, the HKMA organised the Green and Sustainable Banking Conference, providing a platform for the banking and technology sectors to explore the role of low-carbon technologies and green fintech in the net-zero transitions of Hong Kong and the Mainland, while also announcing the results of the Green Fintech Competition. The event attracted around 400 participants from banks, technology companies, regulatory authorities and academia. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green and sustainable finance decision-making, the HKMA developed a local green taxonomy framework with the assistance of a consultant. In May, the HKMA published a discussion paper on the “Prototype of a Green Classification Framework for Hong Kong” to seek stakeholders’ views on the development and implementation of a green taxonomy. Based on the consultation results, the HKMA is refining the prototype framework and identifying additional areas for the next phase of its development. The HKMA participates in the work of the Financial Action Task Force, which has identified environmental crime as a predicate offence for money laundering. Given the interconnections between AML and environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues, this area is receiving increasing attention from regulators. Recognising the potential risks that climate change may pose to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its ongoing surveillance. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps further enrich climate scenarios to enable central banks and supervisors to better understand the macroeconomic and financial implications of climate change. As a member of the Financial Stability Board’s working group on transition planning, the HKMA participates in analysing the interactions between the transition plans of financial and non-financial corporates and financial stability, enabling policymakers to develop a forward-looking and dynamic perspective on climate-related financial risks. On the research front, the HKMA conducts various applied research projects to examine the impact of climate change and broader ESG issues on the financial sector and the economy. Research topics include the climate risk exposures of the banking sector and investment funds2, ESG fund flows3, the impact of climate change on housing prices4, and the ripple effects of corporates’ ESG performance through global supply chains5. The findings of these studies enhance the HKMA’s understanding of the implications of climate change and ESG issues for financial stability and support related policy formulation. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA also shares its research findings with a broad range of stakeholders through various channels, including international events on climate-related issues and the HKMA Research Memorandum series. The HKMA’s “Liquidity Facilities Framework” is a secured standby facility that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. In accordance with the NGFS recommendations, the HKMA has incorporated sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under the framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps facilitate international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, while drawing insights to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA strives to raise market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. During the year, the HKMA worked closely with local and international partners to build a richer ecosystem and further advance green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategies. The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced key initiatives to support Hong Kong in capitalising on sustainable finance opportunities, with major areas of work covering sustainability disclosures, ecosystem building, transition finance and green fintech. Specifically, a Sustainability Disclosures Working Group was established to develop a roadmap for Hong Kong’s adoption of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. The roadmap will cover four key areas, namely sustainability reporting, assurance, data and technology, and skills training. A Transition Finance Working Group was also established to explore ways to support financial institutions and corporates in transition planning and reporting. The Steering Group also strengthened the sustainable finance ecosystem through cross-sectoral capacity building and data enhancement. On data in particular, we continued to promote the adoption of the climate and environmental risk questionnaire for non-listed companies2, launched by the Steering Group in collaboration with CDP in 2022. The Steering Group will continue to keep abreast of the latest developments in green and sustainable finance and enhance Hong Kong’s position as a regional and global green and sustainable finance hub. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced three new key initiatives to capitalise on financing and investment opportunities arising from the low-carbon transition in the Asia-Pacific region. To support capacity building in the industry, the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance under the Steering Group implemented the Government’s Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme, which provides subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates undertaking green and sustainable finance-related training and acquiring relevant qualifications. As of December 2023, a total of 46 international and local training programmes or qualifications had been registered as eligible programmes or qualifications under the Scheme, and more than 560 subsidy applications had been approved. The HKMA also launched the foundation level of a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners. This module aims to foster talent development in the banking industry and enhance the overall professional competence of practitioners. In 2024, the HKMA will continue to collaborate with the banking industry to develop the professional level of the module to meet the industry’s rapidly growing demand for green and sustainable finance professionals. To help financial institutions and corporates, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), better understand key climate- and sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management, sustainability reporting, greenhouse gas emissions calculation and transition planning, the HKMA collaborated during the year with relevant government bureaux and departments as well as global partners including CDP, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ)3 and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF)4 to organise a series of seminars and thematic workshops, attracting participants from the financial services and corporate sectors. For students, following the launch of the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative in 2022, training programmes were held in January and February 2023 to deepen interns’ and university graduates’ understanding of sustainable finance. Recognising the potential of technology to bridge climate-related data gaps and improve data quality, the HKMA strives to make relevant data more accessible and enhance its quality to support informed decision-making and effective climate action. In February 2024, the Steering Group launched a series of website enhancements to provide financial institutions, corporates and the public with a one-stop source of information on green and sustainable finance. Key enhancements included a sustainability disclosure e-platform, greenhouse gas emissions calculation and estimation tools, and more centralised, easily navigable and searchable data and resources. During Hong Kong Green Week, the Steering Group also co-hosted the “Climate Tech for Sustainable Finance” event with Cyberport and Invest Hong Kong to showcase leading green innovation solutions and Hong Kong’s strengths in green technology. Hong Kong Green Week – Finance Stream was held from 26 February to 1 March 2024, during which various sustainability-themed events attracted more than 1,600 participants from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including representatives from financial institutions, corporates, central banks, international organisations, government agencies, academia and consulting firms. The flagship event of Hong Kong Green Week was the Climate Business Forum: Asia Pacific, co-hosted by the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation. The Forum brought together more than 400 participants, including leading decision-makers from the global business and financial communities, to discuss solutions for unlocking climate finance in the Asia-Pacific region. The two-day event explored a broad range of topics, including the energy transition, decarbonisation of heavy industries, the circular economy, the future development of sustainable finance, and emerging climate technologies in Asia-Pacific emerging and developing markets. The Forum received support from public- and private-sector organisations, which co-hosted more than 10 roundtables, seminars and other networking events. Topics covered climate finance, carbon markets, electric vehicle supply chains, financing the net-zero transition, green taxonomies and financing green development in Belt and Road regions. In addition, the HKMA and the International Monetary Fund jointly hosted the Asia Climate Finance Roundtable on 29 February 2024 to discuss key initiatives for scaling up climate finance and the roles of central banks and regulators in managing climate risks. These events formed part of the HKMA’s overall efforts to promote and enrich Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance ecosystem, serving as useful platforms for participants to pursue new business development, share knowledge and explore new opportunities to address climate finance challenges in the Asia-Pacific region. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks5 as a collaborative platform bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop green commercial banking. Since March 2021, the Alliance has held a total of 22 training events and roundtables, attracting more than 7,300 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In October, the Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB published their second thought leadership report, entitled “Developing a High Ambition Climate Strategy for Green Banking: A Case Study”. In October, the Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB jointly published the thought leadership report “Developing a High Ambition Climate Strategy for Green Banking: A Case Study”. During the year, the HKMA Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office joined the newly established Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment (CASI) and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership (GIFP) initiated by the Belt and Road Initiative International Green Development Coalition. Collaboration with CASI and GIFP will facilitate capacity building and knowledge sharing and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects in Asia and beyond. In August 2023, GFANZ announced the establishment of its Hong Kong Chapter to support the net-zero efforts of financial institutions in Hong Kong and the Mainland. The HKMA supports GFANZ’s work in an advisory capacity. To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018. The HKMA assists with green bond issuances under the Programme. To date, the Government has issued approximately US$25 billion equivalent of institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 70 green government projects, such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. The Government continued its regular institutional green bond issuances in the 2023–24 financial year and issued approximately US$6 billion equivalent of green bonds in June. The triple-currency offering covered bonds of various tenors denominated in US dollars, euros and renminbi, attracted a diverse range of investors and received strong subscription demand amounting to nearly US$30 billion equivalent. The issuance size of the renminbi bonds increased from RMB10 billion in January to RMB15 billion, with a 10-year renminbi bond introduced for the first time, helping to extend the Government’s renminbi yield curve and further enrich the range of offshore renminbi products. The enthusiastic response from global investors to the Government’s green bond issuances reflected their recognition of Hong Kong’s commitment to promoting green and sustainable development. In October, the Government issued the second batch of retail green bonds totalling HK$20 billion to further promote market development and financial inclusion. The issuance provided members of the public with an investment opportunity offering stable returns, enabling them to participate in and benefit from the development of green finance in Hong Kong.

As a major global asset owner and manager, the HKMA plays a key role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate agenda. The HKMA has long been a pioneer in responsible investment. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to exercise active ownership and integrate environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “Capital Preservation First, Long-Term Growth”1, the HKMA believes that giving due consideration to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors helps reduce the relevant investment risks while unlocking the long-term sustainable value of investments. As one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and set a “Net-zero by 2050” target2 for its “investment portfolio”, the HKMA is committed to continuously advancing its responsible investment journey, with an emphasis on sustainability, particularly the pressing issue of climate change, with a view to enhancing the resilience of the Exchange Fund and achieving better risk-adjusted long-term returns. As a responsible investor, the HKMA contributes to building a robust green and sustainable finance ecosystem, working with like-minded investors, regulators and international organisations to develop industry standards and promote the adoption of responsible investment across the financial and central banking communities. Through leadership and collaborative initiatives, the HKMA strives to foster a future in which finance and sustainable development go hand in hand. Figure 1 The Exchange Fund’s responsible investment journey Comprehensive and reliable ESG information is essential for integrating sustainability and planning a credible climate transition to achieve net-zero targets. In fulfilment of its commitments to support the Glasgow Declaration3 of the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the Strategic Plan of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, the HKMA leads by example by preparing this chapter on the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the Exchange Fund’s investments. The primary guiding principle sets the tone for the HKMA to pursue responsible investment while taking into account the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, oversees the ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors their implementation through regular reports from the Sustainable Investment Team of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 2, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Strategy Officer, coordinates and oversees the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s various ESG initiatives. Proposals and work progress discussed at the ESG Committee’s quarterly meetings are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition, the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and attended by the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, meets every six months to provide guidance on ESG policies and initiatives across the HKMA’s different functions, including the Exchange Fund Investment Office, in pursuit of the HKMA’s overall ESG objectives. Figure 2 Responsible investment governance structure of the Exchange Fund Investment Office As shown in Figure 1, the Exchange Fund Investment Office embarked on its responsible investment journey in 2016, initially focusing on managing ESG risks that could affect the Exchange Fund’s financial performance. As sustainability evolved rapidly and moved beyond risk considerations to become a strategic priority for major institutions worldwide, the Exchange Fund Investment Office revisited its approach to responsible investment. July 2023 marked another milestone, when the Exchange Fund Investment Office established a new Business Strategy Division led by the Chief Strategy Officer to coordinate and lead its strategic development. The Division incorporates the responsible investment team formerly under the Risk Management and Compliance Division, now known as the Sustainable Investment Team. This strategic move reflects the HKMA’s shift in the focus of responsible investment from a risk-based approach to a more proactive and forward-looking stance in addressing sustainability-related investment issues. The Sustainable Investment Team works closely with different teams within the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists its senior management in managing ESG, particularly climate-related, risks and opportunities across different types of investments: Public market investments — The Credit, Rules and Compliance Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, reviews the integration of ESG factors into credit risk models with input from the Sustainable Investment Team and monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Sustainable Investment Team participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Promoting Active Ownership” under “Risk Management” on page 40 for details). Private market investments — The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal conducted by the private market investment and risk management teams. The HKMA recognises that the physical and transition risks4 arising from climate change, as well as the associated opportunities, may affect the long-term performance and value of the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Emissions Gap Report 20235 published by the United Nations Environment Programme estimates that, unless further reductions in greenhouse gas emissions are made worldwide, the global average temperature will rise by 2.5°C to 2.9°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. The urgent need for more aggressive policies, technological developments or behavioural changes to contain temperature increases may intensify transition risks, such as shocks from asset devaluation or stranded assets. At the same time, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events also pose additional physical risks to investments. The HKMA believes that investing in a greener future is aligned with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives and therefore places particular emphasis on climate-related considerations in ESG integration. The HKMA’s establishment in 2022 of a target for the Exchange Fund’s “investment portfolio” to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier further demonstrates its commitment to the global climate agenda. The HKMA continues to strengthen its three-pronged approach with an explicit focus on decarbonisation and transition. The following sections provide further details of this approach. Figure 3 The HKMA’s three-pronged approach to responsible investment In pursuing its net-zero target, the HKMA favours active engagement over exclusions or divestment from its investible universe. First, maintaining a diversified and robust asset portfolio is crucial to achieving the Exchange Fund’s primary investment objectives. Directly excluding certain sectors or industries would narrow the investible universe, with potential implications for investment returns and risks. By adopting an inclusive approach, the HKMA can capture opportunities to invest in companies undergoing transition and equipped with outstanding technologies and sound corporate governance to address evolving global climate trends, including companies in high-emitting industries. Second, addressing climate change requires the transition of core “brown” industries. Simply excluding or divesting from the relevant investments does not help resolve the issue of carbon emissions. Instead, by deploying strategic capital and exercising active ownership to support these industries, the HKMA encourages them to transition towards sustainable and low-carbon practices, thereby bringing about positive change for both themselves and the world. In response to market developments, the HKMA is refining its net-zero investment strategy to pursue transition outcomes aligned with the Exchange Fund’s and global net-zero objectives through a holistic approach, while adhering to its guiding principles for responsible investment. By integrating ESG factors into investment decisions, the HKMA continues to pursue sustainable investments and opportunities to facilitate climate transition and enhance the long-term resilience of the Exchange Fund’s portfolio (Figure 4). The HKMA’s responsible investment maintained good momentum in 2023. In the public markets, the HKMA launched a new actively managed global equity portfolio themed around sustainability and climate transition, managed by an external investment manager, and extended the use of a customised low-carbon equity index to another externally managed portfolio. In addition, the green, social and sustainability bonds prioritised by the HKMA outperformed their investment benchmark, demonstrating the concept of “doing well by doing good”. In the private markets, the HKMA actively builds resilient portfolios for long-term growth by capturing investment opportunities expected to benefit from long-term economic trends such as the climate and energy transition. For example, during the year the HKMA invested in two Asia-focused transition investment funds, demonstrating its commitment to addressing Asia’s climate transition needs. Unlike conventional chemical recycling systems, which rely on energy-intensive high-temperature environments to produce plastics, the company has pioneered a low-temperature production method powered entirely by solar arrays. Made entirely from waste, this plastic material provides a sustainable and versatile alternative to the petroleum-based resins commonly used in industries such as retail and consumer durables. It is also compatible with existing standard manufacturing processes and cutting-edge technologies such as 3D printing. The company is a staunch supporter of the circular economy. The HKMA committed two tranches of US$1 billion each to the MCPP in 2017 and 2019 respectively, and further collaborated with the IFC in 2021 to create MCPP One Planet, a new global climate-related investment platform and the world’s first Paris-aligned cross-sectoral portfolio of emerging-market loans. Through the MCPP, the HKMA has committed to providing loans to 80 sustainable development projects across 19 sectors, including infrastructure, agriculture, real estate and manufacturing, in 38 developing countries. The HKMA is committed to being a sustainable organisation and adopts a multipronged approach to reducing its carbon footprint, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In addition to promoting environmental sustainability, the HKMA attaches importance to staff well-being and social responsibility, and strives to promote financial inclusion and enhance public financial literacy. As a responsible organisation, the HKMA has set sustainability objectives under three pillars: the environment, its people and social responsibility. The Green and Sustainability Steering Committee (Steering Committee),1 established in October and chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is the principal decision-making body for corporate sustainability initiatives. Formerly known as the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, the Steering Committee leads the HKMA in formulating its vision, strategies and policies on corporate sustainability and social responsibility matters. At the departmental level, the Executive Director (Corporate Services) oversees the implementation of sustainability activities and regularly submits progress reports to the Steering Committee. The Green Office Task Force and the Volunteer Services Team support the coordination of corporate sustainability efforts; the former serves as a platform for exchanging ideas on creating a green workplace, while the latter aims to foster a culture of volunteering. The HKMA has formulated a roadmap to guide its transition. The focus is on implementing decarbonisation strategies in its day-to-day operations, including operating green buildings and data centres, practising green mobility, adopting energy-saving measures, digital tools and greener modes of operation, reducing waste, and building a sustainability culture. The HKMA also plans to use carbon insetting tools within its own value chain to reduce emissions and adopt carbon offsetting measures for hard-to-abate emissions. In addition to the above environmental commitments relating to its day-to-day operations, the HKMA continues to introduce greener operational solutions for the wider community, ranging from channels for banks to submit electronic documents and communicate with the HKMA to electronic payment and coin collection schemes for the general public. To strengthen and sustain its operational capabilities, the HKMA engages a professional workforce, builds a talent pool and places emphasis on staff well-being. In terms of social responsibility, the HKMA encourages staff to participate in volunteering and charitable activities; considers procuring from social enterprises; promotes consumer education on financial services; and works with the banking industry to ensure equitable access to basic banking services across the community. The remainder of this chapter sets out details of the above strategies. Under the HKMA’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Risk Committee,2 chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the potential risks and threats faced by the HKMA in its day-to-day operations, including those arising from climate change. The physical impacts of climate change, such as flooding or other damage caused by more extreme weather events, may affect the HKMA’s offices and impede staff travel. To manage physical risks, the HKMA regularly updates its business continuity plans to address extreme weather conditions. It also conducts regular evacuation and backup facility activation drills to ensure that staff are always prepared to implement business continuity measures. Measures to mitigate potential risks have also been incorporated into office design. Transition risks may affect the HKMA’s energy use, air travel and waste disposal. The HKMA has been monitoring its exposure to transition risks by tracking its greenhouse gas emissions, waste generation, energy consumption and paper use. The HKMA’s climate target is to achieve net-zero Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 (air travel) greenhouse gas emissions across all aspects of its corporate operations by 2050 or earlier. As a near-term emissions reduction target, the HKMA plans to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions by converting all its existing vehicles to electric vehicles, and to reduce Scope 2 emissions intensity by 63% by 2030 or earlier against a 2015 baseline through various decarbonisation and offsetting strategies. Despite the challenges in determining Scope 3 emissions, the HKMA will adopt a multipronged approach, where practicable, to minimise Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions arising from activities such as paper use, waste generation and air travel.
